# Introduction

## Overview

The starting point is a collection of observations about how we interact with the world. We see colours — and always three of them mix to produce white. We can move around, rotate, and look from different angles, yet the things we measure do not depend on where we stand or which way we face. Time flows: the world unfolds, and we drift along that flow. Three-fold structure recurs throughout nature — three colours, three generations of matter, three-fold chirality — in a way that demands explanation rather than stipulation. And crucially, multiple observers share the same world — not each illuminating a private universe, but all navigating a common landscape.

Some observations run deeper. We can measure, record, and compare, and those comparisons are consistent — there is a pairing between what we observe and the instruments we use. Smooth change is the rule: linear approximation describes our universe across scales, from planetary orbits to particle scattering. We can accumulate quantities — add them up, integrate — and we can probe rates of change — take derivatives, differentiate. The universe has *volume*: things occupy space, and that space can be measured. We have the perception of free will and intent — we choose to measure, to act, to organise — and that choice has consequences: observation creates outcomes not determined by the initial conditions. Even the capacity for computation — the ability to reason, count, and calculate — seems woven into the fabric rather than bolted on.

An important assumption this paper does *not* make is that the constants of our universe are indeed constant. If we allow them to vary — in a controlled, algebraic way — how does that change the mechanics — or more precisely, the mechanics of how we observe the quantum universe? This is the question this paper asks.

Einstein showed that geometry and mass are intimately connected: space-time is not a passive stage on which matter performs but a dynamical participant shaped by the matter it contains. This paper extends that insight to the quantum realm. Where general relativity weds curvature to energy–momentum on a smooth manifold, the framework developed here weds *algebraic torsion* — the failure of quantum operations to commute — to the mass and interaction structure of particles, all within a single categorical object.

Heisenberg reminded us that what we observe is not nature itself but nature exposed to our method of questioning. This paper takes that insight seriously. We do not ask what the universe *is* — we ask what its mechanics *do*. Category theory is the natural language for this, because it describes structure and transformation without committing to any particular ontology.

Noether taught us that every continuous symmetry of a physical system yields a conserved quantity. Rotational invariance gives angular momentum; time-translation invariance gives energy; gauge invariance gives charge. This principle is the engine that converts the symmetries we *observe* — the invariances listed above — into the quantities we *measure*. The categorical framework of this paper is driven by that insight: we encode each observed symmetry as structure in a monoidal category, and the Frobenius trace $\int_A$ plays the role of the Noether current — the device that extracts a conserved scalar from each symmetry. As we shall see, the $q$-deformation of the substrate shifts these conservation laws from exact identities to approximate ones, with anomalies that are themselves measurable.

These everyday observations, once stated carefully, determine a specific algebraic structure: a *rigid monoidal category* equipped with a fibre functor and a Frobenius trace $\int_A$. We call this structure a **quantum observable universe** (QOU). Its axioms encode precisely the features listed above and nothing more.

What follows from these axioms is broad in scope and specific in detail. The symmetry group $\mathrm{SU}_2(R)$ is not assumed; it emerges via Tannaka–Krein reconstruction. The uncertainty principle is not postulated; it appears as the geometric signature of degrees of freedom not yet resolved. Observation is an act of intention, and intention can produce genuinely new outcomes — not merely reveal pre-existing ones.

Particles are knots — topological objects classified by their crossing structure — and simultaneously vortex lines in the fibre of the state bundle. These two pictures are not competing descriptions but equivalent viewpoints, exchanged by the Frobenius self-duality $A \cong A^{\vee}$.

Even the capacity for computation — the Turing completeness of the substrate — is a consequence, not an input.

The paper is organised as follows.

[Chapter 1](#chap:qu) introduces the **quantum universe** (QU): the algebraic skeleton encoded in the triple

$$(\mathbf{C},\; A,\; \tau)$$

— a rigid monoidal category $\mathbf{C}$, a Frobenius–Hopf object $A$, and a fibre functor $\tau$. The Frobenius trace $\int_A \colon A \to \mathbf{1}$ is the categorical analogue of integration: it assigns a scalar to each element of the algebra. Combined with the differential calculus (Kähler differentials on $A$), it gives the algebra both the ability to differentiate and to integrate. The Frobenius condition $A \cong A^{\vee}$ — the self-duality of the algebra — says that these two operations are compatible: integrating and then differentiating yields the same result as differentiating and then integrating. Neither path destroys information. From these ingredients the chapter derives the Frobenius relation, the dagger involution, and the Tannaka–Krein reconstruction of the symmetry group.

[Chapter 2](#chap:qou) adds the observability, measurability, and volume axioms that promote the quantum universe to a **quantum observable universe** (QOU). The volume axiom makes the observation from paragraph two precise: the Frobenius trace $\int_A$ is non-degenerate, so the algebra has a well-defined notion of size — volume is not assumed but follows from the interaction of integration and self-duality. The key geometric players emerge: a quantum connection $\theta$, the reconstructed gauge group $G = \mathrm{SU}_2(R)$, and the state bundle $\mathcal{S}$ — so that the QOU is characterised by the archimedean tuple

$$(\mathbf{C},\; \theta,\; G,\; \mathcal{S}).$$

The chapter then constructs a categorical Dirac operator $\mathcal{D}_\nabla$ from the connection and Reeb derivation. Its square decomposes — forced by the Frobenius–Hopf structure, not by assumption — into exactly two curvature terms: one measuring how space itself curves (Ricci), one measuring how the internal gauge field curves (Yang–Mills). Coupling a matter state $\psi$ adds a third. The result is the categorical action

$$\mathcal{S}_q[\nabla, \textstyle\int_A, \psi]
  \;=\;
  \underbrace{\mathrm{tr}\bigl(q \cdot R_{\int}\bigr)}_{\text{gravity}}
  \;+\;
  \underbrace{\textstyle\int_A \!\circ\, \mathrm{tr}_A\bigl(
    F_\nabla \wedge_q \star_q F_\nabla
  \bigr)}_{\text{gauge}}
  \;+\;
  \underbrace{\textstyle\int_A\!\bigl(\psi^{\ast} \cdot \mathcal{D}_\nabla\,\psi\bigr)}_{\text{matter}},$$

constructed entirely from the rigid monoidal structure. Varying this action yields quantum versions of the Einstein, Yang–Mills, and Dirac equations.

[Chapter 3](#chap:torsion) turns to the obstructions that arise when local data is extended to global structures. Measurement constrains observation, and observation constrains what can be lifted from one level of the brane tower to the next. The Yekutieli lifting condition makes this precise: an object admits a lift if and only if its obstruction class $\kappa(x) \in H^2(S, B)$ vanishes. The descent involution $\hat{\tau}$ then decomposes the algebra at each level into descended (observable) and transient (pre-observable) modes. A key result is the Descartes condition $\chi(A) = -6$, forced by the lifting obstructions and the Archimedean constraint. The Kummer exact sequence $1 \to \mu_n \to \mathbb{G}_m \to \mathbb{G}_m \to 1$ filtrates the obstruction space by divisibility: the class $\kappa_0$ persists at all Kummer levels $n \nmid \chi(A)$, a perpetual obstruction that no amount of jet refinement can remove.

[Chapter 4](#chap:path-integrals-braiding) develops a purely mathematical model, built entirely from the categorical data, for objects we call photons, electrons, atoms, and the like. These are associated to knots which, by self-duality, encode not only what the objects *are* but how they interact with one another. The topological mass formula

$$\mathfrak{m}(K) \;=\; \frac{\mathrm{Vol}(K)}{\hbar_q^{\,2}}$$

expresses the mass of a particle knot $K$ in terms of the hyperbolic volume of its complement and the quantum Planck constant $\hbar_q = 1 - 1/q$. The chapter describes explicitly the transfer matrices that govern all particle interactions through a computational cost associated to Skein relations. The embeddability bound on $\Sigma_4$ produces a finite, exhaustive list of exactly $7$ such transfer matrices $T_{\tau(r,s)}(q)$ — six non-trivial force operators and the identity (**interaction completeness**). Physical constants — mass, crossing energy, binding energy — are parametrised solely by $q$. Electronic shells arise as torus knots and their associated representations in Gröbner bases.

[Chapter 5](#chap:models-qou) examines concrete realisations of the QOU axioms: archimedean, $p$-adic, and finite-field models.

[Chapter 6](#chap:descartes-universe) studies Bring’s surface $\Sigma_4$ — the universal genus-$4$ curve with automorphism group $S_5$ — as a model for the Descartes universe ($\chi(A) = -6$). This concrete realisation provides coordinate systems for the red, green, and blue coral tubes — the exceptional divisors where all particle interactions occur — and serves as a model for understanding our own world.

[Chapter 7](#chap:observations) reaps the rewards of the mathematical machinery. The substrate parameter $q$ is estimated from the muon-to-electron mass ratio:

$$(1 - q^{-1})^2 \;=\; \frac{\mathrm{Vol}(4_1)}{m_\mu / m_e}
  \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
  q \;=\; q_0 \;+\; O\!\bigl(2.2 \times 10^{-8}\bigr).$$

From this single parameter we compute estimated masses for all hadrons, which agree to good precision with observed values. The transfer matrices then describe hadron half-lives that align with observation. The same mathematical infrastructure computes the energetics of hydrocarbons.

[The Algebraic Substrate](#chap:algebraic-substrate) develops the spectral theory of the Frobenius–Hopf algebra. The local $q$-zeta function of Bring’s curve encodes the Frobenius eigenvalues; the Hasse–Weil bound confines them to the critical line $|\alpha_i| = q^{1/2}$ — the Riemann hypothesis, proved unconditionally at the $q$-scale. The classical limit functor $\mathcal{L} : \mathbf{C}_q \to \mathbf{C}_1$ is exact but not full: quantum information is lost as $q \to 1$. The obstruction to properties persisting through this limit is a single cohomology class in $HH^2(\mathcal{U}_q, \mathrm{Ad})$, whose dimension the QOU axioms collapse from arbitrary to one — controlled by the Euler characteristic $\chi(A) = -6$ and its Kummer divisibility. The chapter formulates a $q$-deformed Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture: the categorical Mordell–Weil group $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{1}, E_q)$ is trivial (forced by the observability axiom and Tannaka–Krein), so $L(\mathcal{E}_q, 1) \neq 0$ at the $q$-scale. Whether this non-vanishing survives the classical limit is obstructed by the same Kummer tower that controls the Riemann hypothesis.

[Chapter 8](#chap:info-theory) addresses Wigner’s mystery directly. The mechanics of the quantum observable universe turn out to be Turing complete: the combinatorics supporting logic and computation is a property of the algebraic substrate, not the medium. The Gröbner basis ensures this computation is *confluent* — every reduction terminates at the same normal form. The Reeb flow — the internal clock of the algebra — generates a dynamical system whose boundary is a fractal (a Julia set) with Hausdorff dimension

$$d_H(q) = \frac{(2q-1)^2}{q^3}.$$

Crossing energy relates to categorical mass by

$$E_{\mathfrak{H}} = \mathfrak{m}_{\mathfrak{H}} \cdot c_q^{\,2},
  \qquad
  c_q = \frac{1}{q - 1},$$

where $c_q$ is the information speed of light — $E = mc^2$ derived from the categorical structure.

The [Glossary](#chap:glossary) maps paper terminology to Mathlib declarations, the [Knot-Periodic Table](#app:knot-periodic-table) collects the elements with their knot assignments, and the [Index of Definitions](#app:index-definitions) provides a searchable reference to all definitions, theorems, and propositions in the paper.

# Quantum Universes

## Introduction

This chapter introduces the **quantum universe** (QU): a rigid braided monoidal category equipped with a Frobenius–Hopf object, a fibre functor, and a differential calculus. We begin with categorical preliminaries ([§ Rigid monoidal categories](#sec:rigid-monoidal)), state the core axioms ([§ The Quantum Universe](#sec:quantum-universe)), and derive their first consequences — the Frobenius relation, involutive structure, and Tannaka–Krein reconstruction ([§ Consequences](#sec:qu-consequences)).

The QU axioms also support differential-geometric structures: categorical connections, jet objects, and the Hodge star ([§ Structures](#sec:qu-structures)). The passage from a quantum universe to a *quantum observable universe* — adding observability, measurability, and the volume constraint that forces $\mathrm{SU}_2(R)$ as the gauge group — is the subject of [Chapter 2](#chap:qou).

All algebraic groups and projective spaces in this paper are written with their base ring $R$ explicit:

| Object                           | Notation                       | Over $\mathbb{C}$         |
|:---------------------------------|:-------------------------------|:--------------------------|
| Special unitary group            | $\mathrm{SU}_2(R)$             | $\mathrm{SU}(2)$          |
| Maximal torus / Reeb gauge group | $U_1(R)$                       | $U(1)$                    |
| Quantum group                    | $\mathrm{SU}_{q,2}(R)$         | $\mathrm{SU}_q(2)$        |
| Projective line                  | $\mathbb{P}^1(R)$              | $\mathbb{CP}^1 \cong S^2$ |
| Multiplicative group             | $\mathbb{G}_m(R) = R^{\times}$ | $\mathbb{C}^{\times}$     |

When the base ring is clear from context, we may write $\mathrm{SU}_2$ for $\mathrm{SU}_2(R)$ and $\mathbb{P}^1$ for $\mathbb{P}^1(R)$. The category-theoretic definitions ([quantum universe](#def:quantum-universe), [quantum observable universe](#def:quantum-observable-universe)) are formulated over an arbitrary commutative ring $R$ and specialise to any base by substitution. A reader working over $\mathbb{Z}_p$, $\mathbb{F}_q$, or $\mathbb{C}$ reads the same axioms and the same proofs — only the ground ring changes.

## Preliminary: rigid monoidal categories

<div id="def:no-quasi-zeros" class="definition">

**Definition 1.1** (Algebra without quasi-zeros). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.NoQuasiZeros) Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity and let $A$ be an $R$-algebra. An element $a \in A$ is called a **quasi-zero** if*

*$$bac = 0 \qquad \text{for all } b, c \in A \text{ not both } 1.$$*

*We say $A$ is an **algebra without quasi-zeros** if no such element exists. Throughout this paper, whenever $\mathbf{C}$ is $R$-linear we assume that $R$ has no quasi-zeros.*

*This condition appears naturally in the theory of unital Gröbner bases \\}cite{leitnerpawloski2004}, where it ensures that leading-term decompositions are well-defined and the division algorithm terminates correctly. In the categorical setting it guarantees that $R$-linear hom-spaces have no "phantom" morphisms annihilated by all compositions — a necessary condition for the Frobenius pairing to be non-degenerate.*

</div>

<div id="def:snake-identity" class="definition">

**Definition 1.2** (Snake identity). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.snake_identity_left) Let $(\mathbf{C}, \otimes, \mathbf{1})$ be a monoidal category and let $V$ be an object with dual $V^{\vee}$, evaluation $\mathrm{ev} \colon V \otimes V^{\vee} \to \mathbf{1}$, and coevaluation $\mathrm{coev} \colon \mathbf{1} \to V^{\vee} \otimes V$. The **snake identities** (also called *zig-zag identities*) are the two commutative diagrams:*

*$$\label{eq:snake-identities}
\begin{gathered}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2em, column sep=2.5em]
  V
    \ar[r, "\mathrm{id} \otimes \mathrm{coev}"]
    \ar[dr, "\mathrm{id}_V"']
  & V \otimes V^{\vee} \otimes V
    \ar[d, "\mathrm{ev} \otimes \mathrm{id}"]
  \\
  & V
\end{tikzcd}
\\[-0.5em]
\text{\small (left snake identity)}
\end{gathered}
\qquad\qquad
\begin{gathered}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2em, column sep=2.5em]
  V^{\vee}
    \ar[r, "\mathrm{coev} \otimes \mathrm{id}"]
    \ar[dr, "\mathrm{id}_{V^{\vee}}"']
  & V^{\vee} \otimes V \otimes V^{\vee}
    \ar[d, "\mathrm{id} \otimes \mathrm{ev}"]
  \\
  & V^{\vee}
\end{tikzcd}
\\[-0.5em]
\text{\small (right snake identity)}
\end{gathered}$$*

*These identities express the fact that $(\mathrm{ev}, \mathrm{coev})$ exhibit $V^{\vee}$ as a right dual of $V$ (equivalently, that the pair forms an *exact pairing* in the sense of [`CategoryTheory.ExactPairing`](#rem:glossary-exact-pairing)). The terminology "snake" comes from the graphical calculus, where the composites trace out an S-shaped curve that straightens to a vertical line.*

</div>

<div id="def:rigid-monoidal-category" class="definition">

**Definition 1.3** (Rigid monoidal category). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.RigidMonoidalCategory)*

*A **monoidal category** $(\mathbf{C}, \otimes, \mathbf{1})$ is a category equipped with a bifunctor $\otimes \colon \mathbf{C} \times \mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{C}$ (the *tensor product*), a unit object $\mathbf{1}$, and natural isomorphisms expressing associativity and unitality:*

*$$\label{eq:monoidal-axioms}
\begin{gathered}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=3em]
  (X \otimes Y) \otimes Z
    \ar[r, "\alpha_{X,Y,Z}", "\sim"']
  & X \otimes (Y \otimes Z)
\end{tikzcd}
\\[-0.5em]
\text{\small (associativity)}
\end{gathered}
\qquad
\begin{gathered}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.5em]
  \mathbf{1} \otimes X
    \ar[r, "\ell_X", "\sim"']
  & X
  & X \otimes \mathbf{1}
    \ar[l, "\rho_X"', "\sim"]
\end{tikzcd}
\\[-0.5em]
\text{\small (unitality)}
\end{gathered}$$*

*The category is *rigid* if every object $V$ has a *dual* $V^{\vee}$ together with morphisms $\mathrm{ev}_V \colon V \otimes V^{\vee} \to \mathbf{1}$ and $\mathrm{coev}_V \colon \mathbf{1} \to V^{\vee} \otimes V$ satisfying the [snake identities](#def:snake-identity).*

*We say $\mathbf{C}$ is *$R$-linear* (for a commutative ring $R$) if every hom-set is an $R$-module and composition is $R$-bilinear. We require $R$ to be [without quasi-zeros](#def:no-quasi-zeros).*

*The category is *braided monoidal* if it is further equipped with a natural isomorphism (the *braiding*) $c_{X,Y} \colon X \otimes Y \xrightarrow{\sim} Y \otimes X$ compatible with the associator and satisfying the hexagon axioms. When $c_{Y,X} \circ c_{X,Y} = \mathrm{id}$ the braiding is *symmetric*; in general $c^2 \neq \mathrm{id}$. Given a braiding, the *exterior power* $\Lambda^k V$ is defined as the image of the antisymmetriser $\mathrm{Alt}_k = \sum_{\pi \in S_k} \mathrm{sgn}(\pi)\,\pi$ acting on $V^{\otimes k}$, where permutations act via $c$.*

</div>

<div id="ex:rigid-monoidal-vect" class="example">

**Example 1.4** ($\mathbb{C}[z]$ and $\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))$). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.Examples.su2RigidData)*

*The polynomial ring $\mathbb{C}[z]$ is the algebra of functions on the complex line $\mathbb{C}$. The category $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathbb{C}}$ of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces is the simplest $\mathbb{C}$-linear rigid monoidal category: the tensor product is $V \otimes W$, the unit is $\mathbf{1} = \mathbb{C}$, and the dual is $V^{\vee} = \mathrm{Hom}(V, \mathbb{C})$ with $\mathrm{ev}(v \otimes f) = f(v)$.*

*Similarly, the *coordinate ring* $\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))$ is the algebra of polynomial functions on the group $\mathrm{SU}(2)$, generated by the matrix entries $\alpha, \beta, \bar\alpha, \bar\beta$ with $\alpha\bar\alpha + \beta\bar\beta = 1$. The category $\mathbf{C} = \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2))$ of finite-dimensional representations is $\mathbb{C}$-linear rigid monoidal. Its simple objects are the spin-$j$ representations $V_j$ ($j = 0, \tfrac12, 1, \ldots$, $\dim V_j = 2j+1$). The *fundamental object* is $V = V_{1/2} \cong \mathbb{C}^2$.*

</div>

## The Quantum Universe

<div id="def:quantum-universe" class="definition">

**Definition 1.5** (Quantum Universe). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.QuantumUniverse)*

*Let $R$ be a commutative ring. A *quantum universe over $R$* is a triple $(\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)$ where:*

1.  *$(\mathbf{C}, \otimes, \mathbf{1})$ is an $R$-linear rigid braided monoidal category ([rigid monoidal category](#def:rigid-monoidal-category)) with braiding $c_{X,Y} \colon X \otimes Y \xrightarrow{\sim} Y \otimes X$ — the braiding is required for exterior powers $\Lambda^k V$ and need not be symmetric ($c^2 \neq \mathrm{id}$ in general);*

2.  *$A$ is a *Frobenius–Hopf object* in $\mathbf{C}$: an object equipped with morphisms $$\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.5em, column sep=2.5em]
      A \otimes A \ar[r, "\mu"]
      & A \ar[r, "\int_A"]
      & \mathbf{1}
      & {\scriptstyle\text{(multiplication, Frobenius form)}}
      \\
      \mathbf{1} \ar[r, "\eta"]
      & A \ar[r, "\varepsilon"]
      & \mathbf{1}
      & {\scriptstyle\text{(unit, counit)}}
      \\
      A \ar[r, "\Delta"]
      & A \otimes A
      & A \ar[l, "S"']
      & {\scriptstyle\text{(comultiplication, antipode)}}
    \end{tikzcd}$$ — multiplication $\mu$, unit $\eta$, comultiplication $\Delta$, counit $\varepsilon$, antipode $S$, and Frobenius form $\int_A$ — satisfying: **(H)** $(A, \mu, \eta, \Delta, \varepsilon, S)$ is a Hopf algebra object in $\mathbf{C}$; **(F)** the [Frobenius pairing](#def:frobenius-pairing) $\int_A \circ \mu \colon A \otimes A \to \mathbf{1}$ is non-degenerate, inducing an isomorphism $A \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} A^{\vee}$;*

3.  *$\tau \colon \mathbf{C} \to R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$ is a *fibre functor*: an exact, faithful, $R$-linear monoidal functor;*

4.  *$A$ admits a *differential calculus*: the module of K"ahler differentials $\Omega^1(A)$ exists in $\mathbf{C}$.*

</div>

We denote the forgetful (fibre) functor by $\tau$ rather than the more common $\omega$ to avoid conflict with differential-form notation ($\omega_i$ for left-invariant $1$-forms, $\omega_V$ for the vertical curvature form) that appears throughout the paper. The choice of $\tau$ carries several resonances:

- **Tannakian reconstruction.** The letter $\tau$ recalls the Tannaka–Krein theorem that reconstructs the gauge group $G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau)$ from the functor alone.

- **Trace / integration.** In von Neumann algebra theory, a faithful normal state is traditionally denoted $\tau$ (the trace). Since the forgetful functor underlies the Frobenius integration $\int_A$ ([integral notation](#rem:frobenius-integration)), this identification is more than notational.

- **Proper time.** In the archimedean realisation, $\tau$ can be read as the observer’s proper time: the functor parameterises the "emergence" of $R$-modules from the abstract category, turning the static quantum universe into a temporal observable one.

<div id="def:frobenius-pairing" class="definition">

**Definition 1.6** (Frobenius pairing). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.FrobeniusHopfData.frobeniusForm)*

*Let $(\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)$ be a [quantum universe](#def:quantum-universe) with multiplication $\mu \colon A \otimes A \to A$ and Frobenius form $\int_A \colon A \to \mathbf{1}$. The *Frobenius pairing* is the composite*

*$$\label{eq:frobenius-pairing}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.5em]
  A \otimes A \ar[r, "\mu"]
  & A \ar[r, "\int_A"]
  & \mathbf{1}
\end{tikzcd}$$*

*We say the Frobenius pairing is *non-degenerate* when this composite induces an isomorphism $A \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} A^{\vee}$ to the dual object. Equivalently, the snake identities hold: there exists a coevaluation $\tilde{\eta} \colon \mathbf{1} \to A \otimes A$ such that the two composites*

*$$A \xrightarrow{\rho^{-1}} A \otimes \mathbf{1}
  \xrightarrow{\mathrm{id} \otimes \tilde{\eta}} A \otimes A \otimes A
  \xrightarrow{\alpha^{-1}} (A \otimes A) \otimes A
  \xrightarrow{(\int_A \circ \mu) \otimes \mathrm{id}} \mathbf{1} \otimes A
  \xrightarrow{\lambda_A} A$$*

*and its mirror are both equal to $\mathrm{id}_A$.*

</div>

<div id="ex:frobenius-pairing-su2" class="example">

**Example 1.7** (The Frobenius pairing on $\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))$).

*Continuing the SU(2) example ([quantum universe on SU(2)](#ex:quantum-universe-su2)), we make the Frobenius pairing concrete.*

*Set $A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))$ with pointwise multiplication $\mu(f \otimes g) = fg$ and Frobenius form $\int_A f = \int_{\mathrm{SU}(2)} f(g)\,d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar}}(g)$ (the Haar integral). The Frobenius pairing is the composite*

*$$\langle f, g \rangle_A
  \;=\; \int_A \!\circ\, \mu(f \otimes g)
  \;=\; \int_{\mathrm{SU}(2)} f(g)\,h(g)\,d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar}}(g).$$*

*This is the $L^2$ inner product on SU(2).*

***Non-degeneracy.** The pairing is non-degenerate because Haar measure on a compact group has full support: if $\langle f, g \rangle_A = 0$ for all $g \in A$, then $f = 0$ a.e., hence $f = 0$ in $A$. Equivalently, the Peter–Weyl theorem gives an orthonormal basis of matrix coefficients $\{D^j_{mn}\}_{j \in \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}}$ satisfying*

*$$\langle D^j_{mn},\, D^{j'}_{m'n'} \rangle_A
  \;=\; \frac{1}{2j+1}\,\delta_{jj'}\,\delta_{mm'}\,\delta_{nn'}.$$*

*The isomorphism $A \xrightarrow{\sim} A^{\vee}$ sends each basis element to its dual functional scaled by $1/(2j+1)$.*

***Concrete calculation on $\mathbb{C}^2$.** The matrix generators of $\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))$ are $\alpha, \beta, \bar{\alpha}, \bar{\beta}$ with $|\alpha|^2 + |\beta|^2 = 1$. The spin-$\tfrac{1}{2}$ matrix coefficients are $D^{1/2}_{mn} \in \{\alpha, \beta, -\bar{\beta}, \bar{\alpha}\}$. We compute:*

*$$\langle \alpha, \alpha \rangle_A
  \;=\; \int_{\mathrm{SU}(2)} |\alpha|^2\,d\mu
  \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2},
  \qquad
  \langle \alpha, \beta \rangle_A
  \;=\; \int_{\mathrm{SU}(2)} \alpha\,\beta\,d\mu
  \;=\; 0.$$*

*The factor $\tfrac{1}{2} = 1/(2 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2} + 1)$ confirms the Peter–Weyl normalisation for spin $j = \tfrac{1}{2}$.*

***The snake identity** (non-degeneracy in categorical language): the coevaluation $\tilde{\eta} \colon \mathbf{1} \to A \otimes A$ sends $1 \mapsto \sum_{j,m,n} (2j+1)\,D^j_{mn} \otimes \overline{D^j_{mn}}$. The composite $A \xrightarrow{\mathrm{id} \otimes \tilde{\eta}} A \otimes A \otimes A \xrightarrow{(\int_A \circ \mu) \otimes \mathrm{id}} A$ acts as*

*$$f \;\longmapsto\; \sum_{j,m,n} (2j+1)\,
  \langle f,\, D^j_{mn} \rangle_A \cdot \overline{D^j_{mn}}
  \;=\; f,$$*

*by Peter–Weyl completeness. This is $\mathrm{id}_A$, confirming non-degeneracy.*

</div>

<div id="ex:quantum-universe-su2" class="example">

**Example 1.8** ($\mathrm{SU}(2)$ as a quantum universe). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.Examples.su2QuantumUniverse)*

*Continuing [rigid monoidal Vect](#ex:rigid-monoidal-vect), we verify each axiom of [quantum universe](#def:quantum-universe) for $G = \mathrm{SU}(2)$.*

***(i) Category.** $\mathbf{C} = \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2))$, the category of finite-dimensional complex representations. Objects are vector spaces $V$ with a continuous $G$-action $\rho_V \colon G \to \mathrm{GL}(V)$; morphisms are $G$-equivariant linear maps. This is an $\mathbb{C}$-linear rigid monoidal category ([rigid monoidal Vect](#ex:rigid-monoidal-vect)). The $G$-action on tensor products is diagonal: $g \cdot (v \otimes w) = (g \cdot v) \otimes (g \cdot w)$; on duals it is the contragredient: $(g \cdot f)(v) = f(g^{-1} \cdot v)$.*

***(ii) Frobenius–Hopf object.** $A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))$, the coordinate ring of polynomial functions on the group. Its Hopf structure encodes the group operations:*

| *Operation*                            | *Formula*           | *Meaning*                          |
|:---------------------------------------|:--------------------|:-----------------------------------|
| **Multiplication* $\mu(f \otimes g)$*  | *$f \cdot g$*       | *pointwise product of functions*   |
| **Unit* $\eta(1)$*                     | *$1_A$*             | *constant function $1$*            |
| **Comultiplication* $\Delta(f)(x, y)$* | *$f(xy)$*           | *pullback of group multiplication* |
| **Counit* $\varepsilon(f)$*            | *$f(e)$*            | *evaluation at the identity*       |
| **Antipode* $S(f)(x)$*                 | *$f(x^{-1})$*       | *pullback of inversion*            |
| **Frobenius form* $\int_A(f)$*         | *$\int_G f\, d\mu$* | *Haar integration on $G$*          |

*The [Frobenius pairing](#def:frobenius-pairing) $\langle f, g \rangle = \int_A(\mu(f \otimes g)) = \int_G f(x)\, g(x)\, d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar}}(x)$ is positive definite (faithfulness of the Haar integral).*

***(iii) Fibre functor.** $\tau \colon \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) \to \mathrm{Vect}_{\mathbb{C}}$ is the forgetful functor: $\tau(V, \rho) = V$ (forget the $G$-action, keep the vector space). It is exact (short exact sequences of representations split), faithful (a non-zero equivariant map is non-zero as a linear map), and monoidal ($\tau(V \otimes W) = \tau(V) \otimes \tau(W)$). By Tannaka–Krein duality, $G$ can be recovered from $\tau$: $G \cong \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau)$, the group of monoidal natural automorphisms of the fibre functor.*

***(iv) Differential calculus.** The left-invariant calculus on $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ provides $\Omega^1(A) = \mathrm{span}\{\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3\}$, the left-invariant $1$-forms dual to the Lie algebra basis $\{e_1, e_2, e_3\}$ of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ (with $[e_a, e_b] = \epsilon_{abc}\, e_c$; [SU(2) basis](#def:su2-basis)). The universal derivation $d \colon A \to \Omega^1(A)$ acts by $df = \sum_i (\partial_i f)\, \omega_i$, recovering the Lie derivative along each generator.*

</div>

<div id="def:higher-forms" class="definition">

**Definition 1.9** (Higher differential forms). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.HigherForms)*

*Let $(\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)$ be a quantum universe with differential calculus $\Omega^1(A)$ ([quantum universe](#def:quantum-universe)). The *higher differential forms* are the graded $A$-bimodule*

*$$\Omega^k(A) \;=\; \bigwedge\nolimits_A^k \Omega^1(A),
  \qquad k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$$*

*(exterior powers of the $A$-bimodule $\Omega^1(A)$ in $\mathbf{C}$), with $\Omega^0(A) = A$. For an object $V$ in $\mathbf{C}$, $\Lambda^k V$ denotes the $k$-th exterior power of $V$ in the sense of rigid monoidal categories. The differential $d \colon \Omega^k(A) \to \Omega^{k+1}(A)$ extends the universal derivation by the graded Leibniz rule, and satisfies $d^2 = 0$.*

*$$\label{eq:de-rham-complex}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.5em]
  A = \Omega^0(A) \ar[r, "d"]
  & \Omega^1(A) \ar[r, "d"]
  & \Omega^2(A) \ar[r, "d"]
  & \cdots
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad (d^2 = 0)$$*

</div>

<div id="ex:higher-forms-su2" class="example">

**Example 1.10** (Higher forms on $\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))$). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.Examples.su2FormDims)*

*Continuing [quantum universe on SU(2)](#ex:quantum-universe-su2), the left-invariant calculus on $A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))$ has $\Omega^1(A) = \mathrm{span}\{\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3\}$ (three left-invariant $1$-forms, dual to the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{su}(2) = \mathrm{span}\{e_1, e_2, e_3\}$). The higher forms are:*

- *$\Omega^0(A) = A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))$ (functions on the group).*

- *$\Omega^1(A) = A \otimes \mathrm{span}\{\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3\}$ (left-invariant $1$-forms, dimension $3$ over $A$).*

- *$\Omega^2(A) = A \otimes \mathrm{span}\{\omega_1 \wedge \omega_2,\, \omega_1 \wedge \omega_3,\, \omega_2 \wedge \omega_3\}$ (dimension $3$ over $A$).*

- *$\Omega^3(A) = A \otimes \mathrm{span}\{\omega_1 \wedge \omega_2 \wedge \omega_3\}$ (the volume form, dimension $1$ over $A$).*

- *$\Omega^k(A) = 0$ for $k \geq 4$.*

*The differential $d$ is determined by $d\omega_i = -\tfrac{1}{2} \epsilon_{ijk}\,\omega_j \wedge \omega_k$ (the Maurer–Cartan equation of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$).*

</div>

We fix two pieces of notation that will appear throughout.

**The fundamental object $V$.** In a rigid monoidal category $\mathbf{C}$, the *fundamental object* $V$ is the unique (up to isomorphism) simple object of categorical dimension $2$. Its dimension is not an independent assumption: in [Chapter 2](#chap:qou), the volume constraint (a non-degenerate epimorphism $\epsilon \colon \Lambda^2 V \to \mathbf{1}$) forces $\mathrm{rank}(V) = 2$. (If $\mathrm{rank}(V) = 1$ then $\Lambda^2 V = 0$ and no such epimorphism exists; if $\mathrm{rank}(V) \geq 3$ then $\mathrm{rank}(\Lambda^2 V) \geq 3$ and the non-degenerate epimorphism to the rank-$1$ unit object $\mathbf{1}$ cannot exist.) In the SU(2) example ([Example](#ex:rigid-monoidal-vect)), $V = V_{1/2} \cong \mathbb{C}^2$ is the defining (spin-$\tfrac{1}{2}$) representation. Every other simple object $V_j$ is an exterior or symmetric power of $V$, so $V$ generates $\mathbf{C}$ as a tensor category.

**The emergent gauge group $G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau)$.** Let $\tau \colon \mathbf{C} \to R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$ be the forgetful functor. The *tensor automorphism group* $G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau)$ consists of all monoidal natural automorphisms of $\tau$: families of $R$-module automorphisms $\{g_X \colon \tau(X) \xrightarrow{\sim} \tau(X)\}_{X \in \mathbf{C}}$ compatible with the tensor product. By Tannaka–Krein duality, $G$ is an affine group scheme over $R$, and $\tau$ establishes a monoidal equivalence $\mathbf{C} \simeq \mathrm{Rep}(G)$. No group is postulated *a priori*; it *emerges* from $(\mathbf{C}, \tau)$.

## Consequences of the QU axioms

<div id="prop:frobenius-relation" class="proposition">

**Proposition 1.11** (Frobenius relation). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.frobenius_relation)*

*Let $(\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)$ be a ([quantum universe](#def:quantum-universe)). Denote by $\Delta_\mu$ the comultiplication on $A$ dual to the multiplication $\mu$ under the [Frobenius pairing](#def:frobenius-pairing). Then the following diagram commutes (the *Frobenius relation*):*

*$$\label{eq:frobenius-relation}
\begin{gathered}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3.5em]
  A \otimes A
    \ar[r, "\mathrm{id} \otimes \Delta_\mu"]
    \ar[d, "\mu"']
  & A \otimes A \otimes A
    \ar[d, "\mu \otimes \mathrm{id}"]
  \\
  A \ar[r, "\Delta_\mu"']
  & A \otimes A
\end{tikzcd}
\\[-0.5em]
\text{\small Frobenius relation: } (\mu \otimes \mathrm{id}) \circ (\mathrm{id} \otimes \Delta_\mu) = \Delta_\mu \circ \mu
\end{gathered}$$*

*That is, sliding a multiplication past a comultiplication (or vice versa) yields the same result as composing them: $(\mu \otimes \mathrm{id}) \circ (\mathrm{id} \otimes \Delta_\mu) = \Delta_\mu \circ \mu$.*

</div>

<div class="proof">

*Proof of Frobenius relation.* <span id="prf:frobenius-relation" label="prf:frobenius-relation"></span>

The Frobenius form $\int_A$ and the multiplication $\mu$ together define a pairing $\langle a, b \rangle = \int_A(\mu(a \otimes b))$ on $A$. Non-degeneracy of this pairing ([Frobenius pairing](#def:frobenius-pairing)) gives an isomorphism $\phi \colon A \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} A^{\vee}$ defined by $\phi(a) = \langle a, - \rangle$. Define the *dual comultiplication* $\Delta_\mu$ as the transpose of $\mu$ under $\phi$:

$$\Delta_\mu = (\phi^{-1} \otimes \phi^{-1}) \circ \mu^{\vee} \circ \phi,$$

where $\mu^{\vee} \colon A^{\vee} \to A^{\vee} \otimes A^{\vee}$ is the linear dual of $\mu$.

To verify the Frobenius relation, consider the two composites $(\mu \otimes \mathrm{id}) \circ (\mathrm{id} \otimes \Delta_\mu)$ and $\Delta_\mu \circ \mu$ as maps $A \otimes A \to A \otimes A$. It suffices to show they agree after pairing with an arbitrary test element $c \in A$ via $\int_A$, since the pairing is non-degenerate.

For the left-hand side, using the definition of $\Delta_\mu$ and the associativity of $\mu$:

$$\bigl\langle (\mu \otimes \mathrm{id})
  (\mathrm{id} \otimes \Delta_\mu)(a \otimes b),\; c \bigr\rangle
  = \int_A \mu\bigl(\mu(a \otimes b_1) \otimes b_2\bigr) \cdot c
  = \int_A \mu\bigl(a \otimes \mu(b_1 \otimes b_2)\bigr) \cdot c,$$

where $\Delta_\mu(b) = b_1 \otimes b_2$ (Sweedler notation) and the second equality is associativity of $\mu$.

For the right-hand side:

$$\bigl\langle \Delta_\mu(\mu(a \otimes b)),\; c \bigr\rangle
  = \int_A \mu\bigl(a \otimes \mu(b_1 \otimes b_2)\bigr) \cdot c.$$

Both sides equal the same expression, so the Frobenius relation holds. The key step is that $\Delta_\mu$ is defined as the transpose of $\mu$, and associativity of $\mu$ — the only non-trivial axiom used — ensures the two ways of "sliding" multiplication past comultiplication agree. ◻

</div>

<div id="def:involutive-structure" class="definition">

**Definition 1.12** (Involutive structure ($\ast$-structure)). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.InvolutiveStructure)*

*Let $(\mathbf{C}, \otimes, \mathbf{1})$ be an $R$-linear rigid monoidal category. An *involutive structure* (also called a *$\ast$-structure* or *dagger structure*) on $\mathbf{C}$ is a contravariant endofunctor $\dagger \colon \mathbf{C}^{\mathrm{op}} \to \mathbf{C}$ satisfying:*

1.  ***Identity on objects:** $X^{\dagger} = X$ for every object $X$.*

2.  ***Involutivity:** $f^{\dagger\dagger} = f$ for every morphism $f$, depicted: $$\label{eq:involutivity-cd}
    \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=3em]
      X \ar[r, "f"] \ar[rr, bend left=30, "f^{\dagger\dagger} = f"]
      & Y \ar[r, "f^{\dagger}"{description}]
      & X
    \end{tikzcd}$$*

3.  ***Monoidal compatibility:** $(\mathrm{id}_X \otimes f)^{\dagger} = \mathrm{id}_X \otimes f^{\dagger}$, i.e. the following square commutes: $$\label{eq:monoidal-dagger-cd}
    \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em]
      X \otimes Y \ar[r, "\mathrm{id} \otimes f"]
        \ar[d, "(\mathrm{id} \otimes f)^{\dagger}"']
      & X \otimes Z \ar[d, "\mathrm{id} \otimes f^{\dagger}"] \\
      X \otimes Z \ar[r, equal]
      & X \otimes Z
    \end{tikzcd}$$*

4.  ***Contravariance:** $(g \circ f)^{\dagger} = f^{\dagger} \circ g^{\dagger}$: $$\label{eq:dagger-contravariance}
    \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=3em]
      X \ar[r, "f"] & Y \ar[r, "g"] & Z
    \end{tikzcd}
    \quad\xmapsto{\;\dagger\;}\quad
    \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=3em]
      Z \ar[r, "g^{\dagger}"] & Y \ar[r, "f^{\dagger}"] & X
    \end{tikzcd}
    \qquad\text{(contravariance)}$$*

*For the Hopf algebra $A$ in a quantum universe, the antipode $S$ provides a natural involutive structure on the representation category via $f^{\dagger} = \int_A \circ \mu(S(f) \otimes -)$. In the $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ example, this is the Hilbert-space adjoint ([dagger on SU(2)](#ex:dagger-su2)).*

</div>

<div id="prop:positive-definite-dagger" class="proposition">

**Proposition 1.13** (Frobenius dagger is positive-definite). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.frobenius_dagger_positive_definite)*

*Let $(\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)$ be a [quantum universe](#def:quantum-universe) with [Frobenius pairing](#def:frobenius-pairing) $\langle a, b \rangle = \int_A(\mu(a \otimes b))$ and antipode $S$. Define the *Frobenius dagger* on morphisms by*

*$$f^{\dagger} \;=\; \int_A \circ \mu(S(f) \otimes -).$$*

*Then $\dagger$ is a positive-definite involutive structure on $\mathbf{C}$: for every non-zero morphism $f \colon \mathbf{1} \to X$, the composite $f^{\dagger} \circ f$ is a positive element of $\mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}) \cong R$.*

</div>

<div class="proof">

*Proof that the Frobenius dagger is positive-definite.* <span id="prf:positive-definite-dagger" label="prf:positive-definite-dagger"></span>

**Involutivity.** The antipode of a Hopf algebra satisfies $S^2 = \mathrm{id}$ (since the Frobenius pairing forces $A$ to be commutative via faithfulness of $\tau$). Therefore $f^{\dagger\dagger} = \int_A \circ \mu(S(S(f)) \otimes -) = \int_A \circ \mu(f \otimes -) = f$, confirming $\dagger$ is an involution.

**Contravariance.** For composable morphisms $f, g$: $(g \circ f)^{\dagger} = \int_A \circ \mu(S(g \circ f) \otimes -) = \int_A \circ \mu(S(f) \cdot S(g) \otimes -)$ since $S$ is an anti-homomorphism. The Frobenius associativity then gives $f^{\dagger} \circ g^{\dagger}$.

**Positive-definiteness.** Let $f \colon \mathbf{1} \to X$ be non-zero. The composite $f^{\dagger} \circ f \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}) \cong R$ evaluates as

$$f^{\dagger} \circ f
  \;=\; \int_A \mu(S(f) \otimes f)
  \;=\; \int_A |f|^2$$

where $|f|^2 = S(f) \cdot f = \overline{f} \cdot f$ under the identification $S = \overline{(\cdot)}$ on functions. Since $\int_A$ is the categorical integral (non-degenerate by the Frobenius axiom) and $|f|^2 \neq 0$ for $f \neq 0$ (faithfulness of $\tau$), the result is a positive element of $R$. ◻

</div>

## Structures on a Quantum Universe

<div id="def:categorical-connection" class="definition">

**Definition 1.14** (Categorical connection and curvature). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.CategoricalConnection)*

*Let $(\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)$ be a quantum universe over $R$ with differential forms $\Omega^k(A)$ ([higher forms](#def:higher-forms)).*

*A *connection* on $A$ is a morphism $\nabla \colon A \to A \otimes \Omega^1(A)$ in $\mathbf{C}$ satisfying the Leibniz rule: $\nabla(\mu(a \otimes b)) = \nabla(a) \cdot b + a \cdot \nabla(b)$, expressed by the commutativity of the *Leibniz triangle*:*

*$$\label{eq:leibniz-triangle}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3.5em]
  A \otimes A
    \ar[r, "\mu"]
    \ar[dr, "{\nabla \otimes 1 \,+\, 1 \otimes \nabla}"']
  & A \ar[d, "\nabla"]
  \\
  & A \otimes \Omega^1(A)
\end{tikzcd}$$*

*The *curvature* of $\nabla$ is the composition*

*$$\label{eq:curvature-composition}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=3em]
  A \ar[r, "\nabla"]
  & A \otimes \Omega^1(A) \ar[r, "\nabla"]
  & A \otimes \Omega^2(A)
\end{tikzcd}$$*

*denoted $F_\nabla = \nabla^2$, which is $A$-linear (a standard consequence of the Leibniz rule).*

</div>

<div id="def:categorical-jet" class="definition">

**Definition 1.15** (Categorical jet object). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.CategoricalJet)*

*Let $(\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)$ be a ([quantum universe](#def:quantum-universe)) with connection $\nabla$ ([categorical connection](#def:categorical-connection)). The *jet object* is*

*$$J^1(A) := A \otimes_{\mathbf{C}} \Omega^1(A),$$*

*where $\Omega^1(A) = \ker(\mu \colon A \otimes A \to A)$ is the bimodule of K"ahler differentials. The jet object fits into the universal extension*

*$$\label{eq:jet-ses}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.5em]
  0 \ar[r]
  & A \otimes \Omega^1(A) \ar[r]
  & J^1(A) \ar[r, "j^1"]
  & A \ar[r]
  & 0
\end{tikzcd}$$*

*where $j^1 \colon J^1(A) \to A$ is the jet evaluation (the counit of the tensor–hom adjunction).*

</div>

<div id="def:categorical-hodge-star" class="definition">

**Definition 1.16** (Categorical Hodge star). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.CatHodgeInvolution)*

*Let $(\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)$ be a quantum universe over $R$ ([quantum universe](#def:quantum-universe)) with higher differential forms $\Omega^k(A)$ ([higher forms](#def:higher-forms)). The *categorical Hodge star* is the involution $\star \colon \Omega^k(A) \to \Omega^{n-k}(A)$ defined by*

*$$\alpha \wedge \star \beta
  = \int_A\!\bigl(\alpha^* \cdot \beta\bigr)\;\mathrm{vol},$$*

*$$\label{eq:categorical-hodge-diagram}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em]
  \Omega^k(A) \ar[r, "\star"] \ar[d, "\star"']
  & \Omega^{n-k}(A) \ar[d, "\star"] \\
  \Omega^{n-k}(A) \ar[r, equal]
  & \Omega^{n-k}(A)
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad (\star^2 = \mathrm{id})$$*

*where $\int_A \colon A \to \mathbf{1}$ is the Frobenius form, $\alpha^* = S(\alpha)$ is the antipode-conjugate, and $\mathrm{vol} \in \Omega^n(A)$ is the volume form (the unique $G$-invariant top form normalised by $\int_A(\mathrm{vol}) = 1$). That $\star^2 = \mathrm{id}$ (i.e. $\star$ is an involution) follows from the non-degeneracy of $\int_A$ and the involutivity of the antipode. More precisely: $S^2 = \mathrm{id}$ holds on $A$ because a commutative Hopf algebra has involutive antipode (and our Frobenius–Hopf axioms imply commutativity of $A$ via the faithfulness of $\tau$ into $R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$). The extension to $\Omega^k(A)$ follows from the graded Leibniz rule for $S$ on the differential graded algebra.*

</div>

<div id="ex:hodge-su2" class="example">

**Example 1.17** (Hodge star on $\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))$). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.Examples.su2Hodge)*

*Continuing [higher forms on SU(2)](#ex:higher-forms-su2), the Hodge star on $A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))$ acts on the $3D$-calculus $\Omega^{\bullet}(A)$ as follows. The volume form is $\mathrm{vol} = \omega_1 \wedge \omega_2 \wedge \omega_3$ (normalised by $\int_A(\mathrm{vol}) = 1$). Then:*

- *$\star 1 = \mathrm{vol}$, $\star\mathrm{vol} = 1$.*

- *On $1$-forms: $\star\omega_i = \tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon_{ijk}\, \omega_j \wedge \omega_k$ (each basis form maps to its complementary $2$-form).*

- *On $2$-forms: $\star(\omega_i \wedge \omega_j) = \epsilon_{ijk}\,\omega_k$ (each basis $2$-form maps to its complementary $1$-form).*

*The Hodge star is the categorical version of "rotating a form into its complement": it identifies $\Omega^k(A)$ with $\Omega^{n-k}(A)$ using the Frobenius form as the inner product. The self-dual $2$-forms $\Omega^+(A)$ are the $+1$-eigenspace of $\star$; in $3$ dimensions, $\star$ on $\Omega^2(A)$ maps to $\Omega^1(A)$, so the self-dual/anti-self-dual decomposition is trivial. The non-trivial decomposition arises when $\dim H = 4$ (the archimedean case, [self-dual curvature](#ex:self-dual-curvature)).*

</div>

# Quantum Observable Universes

## The Quantum Observable Universe

<div id="def:quantum-observable-universe" class="definition">

**Definition 2.1** (Quantum Observable Universe). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.QuantumObservableUniverse)*

*A quantum universe $(\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)$ over $R$ ([quantum universe](#def:quantum-universe)) is *observable* if the forgetful functor $\tau$ ([Example](#ex:rigid-monoidal-vect)) is faithful and the following conditions hold:*

1.  **(non-degenerate integration)* the Frobenius form $\int_A \colon A \to \mathbf{1}$ induces a non-degenerate pairing $(a, b) \mapsto \int_A ab$ ([Frobenius pairing](#def:frobenius-pairing)), giving an isomorphism $A \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} A^{\vee}$;*

2.  **(observability)* there are no hidden global symmetries: $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{1},\, \mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0$, where $\mathrm{Ad}(A)$ is the adjoint object ($A$ acted on by conjugation). Physically, this means every internal degree of freedom is accessible to measurement — no gauge transformation acts trivially on all observables. The formal statement is that every morphism $\mathbf{1} \to \mathrm{Ad}(A)$ is zero: $$\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.5em]
      \mathbf{1} \ar[r, "0"] & \mathrm{Ad}(A)
    \end{tikzcd}
    \qquad\text{(observability)}$$*

3.  **(measurability / anomaly-free)* the primary Chern classes of the adjoint object vanish. Precisely, define the *Chern classes of a categorical object* $X$ by pulling back through the fibre functor: $$c_i(X) \;:=\; c_i\!\bigl(\tau(X)\bigr)
      \;\in\; H^{2i}_{\mathrm{dR}}\!\bigl(\mathrm{Spec}\,R\bigr),$$ where the right-hand side is the classical Chern class of the realised $R$-module (or, in the archimedean setting, of the associated vector bundle $\tau(X) \times_G M$). This definition is intrinsic to the pair $(\mathbf{C}, \tau)$ — the fibre functor $\tau$ is part of the QOU datum — and reduces to the standard topological Chern classes in every geometric realisation. The measurability axiom requires: $$c_1(\mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0
      \qquad\text{and}\qquad
      c_2(\mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0.$$ The first condition ensures the adjoint bundle is orientable, precluding global anomalies; the second ensures the volume form acquires no topological phases (see [Remark](#rem:yekutieli-stokes-remark) for the connection to categorical flatness via Yekutieli’s nonabelian Stokes theorem). For many applications, axioms (1), (2), and (3) suffice — axiom (3) is needed only when global topology of $M$ matters.*

4.  **(categorical volume constraint)* let $V$ denote the fundamental object of $\mathbf{C}$ ([Remark](#rem:fundamental-object-explication)); there exists a non-degenerate epimorphism $\epsilon$ preserved by the rigid dualities, making the following diagram commute for every $g \in \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau)$: $$\label{eq:categorical-volume-constraint}
    \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em]
      \Lambda^2 V \ar[r, "\Lambda^2 g_V"]
                  \ar[d, "\epsilon"', two heads]
      & \Lambda^2 V \ar[d, "\epsilon", two heads]
      \\
      \mathbf{1} \ar[r, "g_{\mathbf{1}} = \mathrm{id}"']
      & \mathbf{1}
    \end{tikzcd}
    \qquad\text{(volume constraint)}$$*

*The braiding $c_{V,V}$ on $\mathbf{C}$ (which is non-symmetric: $c_{V,V}^2 \neq \mathrm{id}$, since $\mathbf{C}$ is braided monoidal but not symmetric monoidal) induces a canonical admissible well-ordering on the Hecke basis. See [braiding-induced ordering](#prop:braiding-induced-ordering).*

</div>

<div id="prop:braiding-induced-ordering" class="proposition">

**Proposition 2.2** (The braiding induces a canonical admissible well-ordering on the Hecke basis). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.braiding_induced_ordering)*

***Proposition.** *Let $(\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)$ be a quantum observable universe ([QOU](#def:quantum-observable-universe)) whose braiding $c_{V,V} \colon V \otimes V \to V \otimes V$ is non-symmetric ($c_{V,V}^2 \neq \mathrm{id}$). Then $c_{V,V}$ determines a canonical admissible well-ordering $\prec_c$ on the monomial basis $B$ of the Hecke algebra $H_n(q)$ of $A$.**

***Construction.** The monomial basis $B$ of $H_n(q)$ consists of reduced positive braid monomials $w = \sigma_{i_1}\sigma_{i_2}\cdots\sigma_{i_k}$ — the images of the braiding $c_{V,V}$ under $\rho_n(\sigma_i) = \mathrm{id}^{\otimes(i-1)} \otimes c_{V,V} \otimes \mathrm{id}^{\otimes(n-i-1)}$ ([braid action on tensor powers](#prop:braid-action-tensor)). The braiding $c_{V,V}$ (as opposed to its inverse $c_{V,V}^{-1}$) defines "positive crossing" — forward time.*

**Definition.* A **well-ordering** on a set $S$ is a total order $\prec$ such that every non-empty subset of $S$ has a least element. Equivalently: there are no infinite strictly descending chains $s_1 \succ s_2 \succ s_3 \succ \cdots$.*

**Definition.* The **degree-lexicographic ordering** $\prec_c$ on $B$ is: $w \prec_c w'$ if and only if*

*$$\ell(w) < \ell(w'),
  \quad\text{or}\quad
  \ell(w) = \ell(w') \;\text{and}\;
  (i_1, \ldots, i_k) <_{\mathrm{lex}} (i_1', \ldots, i_k')$$*

*where $\ell(w) = k$ is the word length (number of crossings) and $<_{\mathrm{lex}}$ is lexicographic order on the generator indices $i_j \in \{1, \ldots, n-1\}$.*

**Proof that $\prec_c$ is a well-ordering on $B$.* Let $S \subseteq B$ be non-empty.*

*(a) **Degree is bounded below.** Every $w \in B$ has $\ell(w) \geq 0$. Let $d = \min\{\ell(w) : w \in S\}$. The set $S_d = \{w \in S : \ell(w) = d\}$ is non-empty.*

*(b) **Finite alphabet at each degree.** Each $w \in S_d$ is a word of length $d$ over the finite alphabet $\{1, \ldots, n-1\}$. There are at most $(n-1)^d$ such words — a finite set. Every finite totally ordered set has a minimum. Let $w_0$ be the lex-minimum of $S_d$.*

*(c) **$w_0$ is the minimum of $S$.** For any $w \in S$: if $\ell(w) > d$ then $w_0 \prec_c w$ (shorter words first); if $\ell(w) = d$ then $w_0 \leq_{\mathrm{lex}} w$ by construction. $\square$*

**Admissibility.* The ordering $\prec_c$ is **admissible** in the sense of ([admissible system](#def:admissible-system)): left and right multiplication by basis elements preserves the ordering ($w \prec_c w'$ implies $u \cdot w \cdot v \prec_c u \cdot w' \cdot v$ whenever both products are non-zero), because degree-lex is compatible with any associative multiplication whose defining relations (Hecke, Yang–Baxter) have leading terms of bounded degree — the Hecke relation is quadratic.*

***Two faces of the arrow of time.** The braiding $c_{V,V}$ and the Reeb vector field $\xi$ ([categorical Reeb](#def:categorical-reeb)) express the same arrow of time from two complementary viewpoints:*

- ***Categorical arrow** ($c_{V,V}$): which strand crosses *over*. A positive crossing $\sigma_i$ applies $c_{V,V}$; a negative crossing $\sigma_i^{-1}$ applies $\bar{c}_{V,V} := c_{V,V}^{-1}$. The ordering $\prec_c$ is the algebraic encoding: forward time = Gröbner reduction under $\prec_c$.*

- ***Geometric arrow** ($\xi$): which direction the Reeb flow runs. The one-parameter subgroup $\phi_t^q$ generated by $\xi$ is the flow of forward time on the state bundle $\mathcal{S}$. At each Planck step, one application of $c_{V,V}$ advances $\phi_t^q$ by one tick.*

***Crossing reversal = time reversal.** The crossing reversal involution $\sigma \colon K \mapsto K^{\sigma}$ (mirror all crossings) corresponds to switching the braiding: $c_{V,V} \leftrightarrow \bar{c}_{V,V}$. This flips the ordering $\prec_c$ and reverses the Reeb flow $\xi \mapsto -\xi$. In the Feynman–Stueckelberg interpretation, an antiparticle ($K^{\sigma}$) is its particle ($K$) with time reversed — precisely the opposite braiding. CPT symmetry is the statement that the QOU axioms are invariant under simultaneous $c_{V,V} \leftrightarrow \bar{c}_{V,V}$ (T), $K \mapsto K^{\sigma}$ (C), and $\sigma_i \mapsto \sigma_{n-i}$ (P, strand reflection).*

</div>

The Frobenius form $\int_A \colon A \to \mathbf{1}$ extends to a pairing on products:

$$\int_A ab \;:=\; \int_A \!\circ\; \mu(a \otimes b).$$

The non-degeneracy condition (i) of [quantum observable universe](#def:quantum-observable-universe) then reads: the pairing $(a, b) \mapsto \int_A ab$ induces an isomorphism $A \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} A^{\vee}$.

Readers familiar with TQFT will recognise $\int_A$ as a categorical Haar measure: the unique (up to scalar) $G$-invariant functional on $A$. The existence of the volume $\epsilon$ ([categorical volume constraint](#eq:categorical-volume-constraint)) may then be read as the normalisation condition $\int_A \mathbf{1}$ is a well-defined topological constant.

<div id="rem:yekutieli-stokes" class="remark">

**Remark 2.3** (Nonabelian Stokes and the measurability conditions).

*The measurability condition $c_1(\mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0$, $c_2(\mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0$ can be understood through the lens of Yekutieli’s nonabelian Stokes theorem \\}cite{yekutieli2015}. The core of that theorem is: for a nonabelian integral to be well-defined over a surface or volume, the curvature of the connection must vanish (or be highly constrained).*

*In the QOU setting, the vanishing of $c_1(\mathrm{Ad}(A))$ imposes a *categorical flatness* on the adjoint representation — the condition required for the parallel transport around a boundary to be path-independent. The existence of the volume $\epsilon$ ([categorical volume constraint](#eq:categorical-volume-constraint)) can therefore be viewed as a categorical realisation of the nonabelian Stokes theorem: the flatness conditions guarantee the global coherence of the volume form.*

*The additional condition $c_2(\mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0$ ensures that $\epsilon$ is canonically unique and does not acquire topological phases under transport around non-contractible cycles. Together, the two vanishing conditions make $\mathrm{Ad}(A)$ *anomaly-free*: the adjoint bundle carries no hidden topological obstructions to integration.*

</div>

<div id="ex:qou-su2" class="example">

**Example 2.4** ($\mathrm{SU}(2)$ is observable). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.Examples.su2Observable)*

*Continuing [Examples](#ex:rigid-monoidal-vect) and [quantum universe on SU(2)](#ex:quantum-universe-su2), write $V = V_{1/2} \cong \mathbb{C}^2$:*

1.  **Non-degeneracy.* The Haar integral $\int_A = \int_G$ on $\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))$ is faithful: if $\int_A(f^* f) = 0$ then $f = 0$.*

2.  **Observability.* The adjoint representation $\mathrm{Ad} \cong V_1$ (spin-$1$, dimension $3$) is irreducible, so it contains no copy of the trivial representation: $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{1}, V_1) = 0$.*

3.  **Volume constraint.* For $v, w \in V = \mathbb{C}^2$, the determinant $\epsilon(v \wedge w) = v_1 w_2 - v_2 w_1$ defines a non-degenerate map $\epsilon \colon \Lambda^2 V \to \mathbb{C}$.*

</div>

## Emergence from observability

<div id="ex:frobenius-su2" class="example">

**Example 2.5** (Frobenius relation for $\mathrm{SU}(2)$). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.Examples.su2Frobenius)*

*Continuing [QOU on SU(2)](#ex:qou-su2), set $A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))$ with multiplication $\mu(f \otimes g) = fg$ (pointwise product) and Frobenius form $\int_A = \int_G$ (Haar integral). The dual comultiplication is $\Delta_\mu(f)(g,h) = \int_G f(xg)\,\overline{h(x)}\,dx$, and the Frobenius relation expresses the associativity of convolution: $\int_G f(xy)\,g(y)\,dy$ can be evaluated by convolving first with $f$ or first with $g$.*

</div>

<div id="ex:dagger-su2" class="example">

**Example 2.6** (Involutive structure on $\mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2))$). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.Examples.su2Dagger)*

*Continuing [Frobenius SU(2)](#ex:frobenius-su2), the category $\mathbf{C} = \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2))$ carries a canonical involutive structure built from the antipode:*

- **What it does.* For a morphism $f \colon V_j \to V_k$ (an equivariant linear map between representations), $f^{\dagger}$ is the *Hilbert-space adjoint*: the unique map $f^{\dagger} \colon V_k \to V_j$ satisfying $\langle f^{\dagger}(w),\, v \rangle_j = \langle w,\, f(v) \rangle_k$ for all $v \in V_j$, $w \in V_k$.*

- **Why it exists.* Each irreducible representation $V_j$ carries a unique (up to scalar) $\mathrm{SU}(2)$-invariant inner product. The adjoint $f^{\dagger}$ with respect to these inner products is automatically equivariant, so $f^{\dagger}$ is again a morphism in $\mathbf{C}$.*

- **On the algebra.* On $A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))$, $f^{\dagger} = \int_A \circ \mu(S(f) \otimes -)$, where $S(f)(g) = f(g^{-1})$ is the antipode. The involution $f \mapsto f^{\dagger}$ is complex conjugation composed with pullback by inversion: $f^{\dagger}(g) = \overline{f(g^{-1})}$.*

- **Positive-definiteness.* For a non-zero state $f \colon \mathbb{C} \to V_j$, the composite $f^{\dagger} \circ f = \lVert f(1) \rVert^2 > 0$. This is the statement that the inner product on each $V_j$ is positive-definite — the categorical encoding of unitarity.*

</div>

<div id="lem:volume-from-rigidity" class="lemma">

**Lemma 2.7** (Volume form from rigidity and symplectic self-duality). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.volume_from_rigidity)*

*Let $(\mathbf{C}, \otimes, \mathbf{1})$ be an $R$-linear rigid monoidal category, and let $V$ be a simple object that is *symplectically self-dual*: there exists an isomorphism $\phi \colon V \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} V^{\vee}$ satisfying $\phi^{\vee} = -\phi$ (alternating). The alternating condition forces $\mathrm{rank}(V) = 2$: the composite $\mathrm{ev}_V \circ (\mathrm{id} \otimes \phi)$ factors through $\Lambda^2 V$, and for the resulting morphism $\epsilon \colon \Lambda^2 V \to \mathbf{1}$ to be a non-degenerate epimorphism one needs $\mathrm{rank}(\Lambda^2 V) = 1$, i.e., $\mathrm{rank}(V) = 2$. The factorisation is (the *volume form factorisation*):*

*$$\label{eq:volume-form-factorisation}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em]
  V \otimes V
    \ar[r, "\mathrm{id} \otimes \phi"]
    \ar[d, "\pi"', two heads]
  & V \otimes V^{\vee}
    \ar[d, "\mathrm{ev}_V"]
  \\
  \Lambda^2 V
    \ar[r, "\epsilon"', dashed]
  & \mathbf{1}
\end{tikzcd}$$*

*and $\epsilon$ is non-degenerate; that is, condition (iii) of [quantum observable universe](#def:quantum-observable-universe) holds.*

</div>

<div class="proof">

*Proof of Volume form from rigidity and symplectic self-duality.* <span id="prf:volume-from-rigidity" label="prf:volume-from-rigidity"></span>

Because $\phi$ is alternating, the pairing $B = \mathrm{ev}_V \circ (\mathrm{id} \otimes \phi)$ satisfies $B \circ \tau_{V,V} = -B$, where $\tau_{V,V}$ is the symmetry (or braiding) isomorphism. Hence $B$ vanishes on symmetric tensors and factors as $B = \epsilon \circ \pi$, where $\pi \colon V \otimes V \twoheadrightarrow \Lambda^2 V$ is the canonical projection. Non-degeneracy of $\epsilon$ follows from non-degeneracy of $\mathrm{ev}_V$ (guaranteed by rigidity) and the isomorphism $\phi$. The duality axioms $(\mathrm{ev}_V \otimes \mathrm{id}) \circ (\mathrm{id} \otimes \mathrm{coev}_V) = \mathrm{id}_V$ ensure that $\epsilon$ is preserved by the rigid dualities of $\mathbf{C}$. ◻

</div>

<div id="ex:su2-volume-from-rigidity" class="example">

**Example 2.8** ($\mathrm{SU}(2)$ volume form from the lemma).

*Continuing [QOU on SU(2)](#ex:qou-su2), take $V = V_{1/2} \cong \mathbb{C}^2$. The symplectic form is $\phi = \begin{smallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{smallmatrix}$, identifying $V \cong V^{\vee}$ with $\phi^{\vee} = -\phi$ (alternating). [volume from rigidity](#lem:volume-from-rigidity) then gives:*

- *The evaluation pairing becomes $B(v, w) = v_1 w_2 - v_2 w_1$ (the determinant).*

- *$B$ is alternating, so it factors through $\Lambda^2 V$: the map $\epsilon \colon \Lambda^2 V \to \mathbb{C}$ is $\epsilon(v \wedge w) = \det(v, w)$.*

- *Non-degeneracy: $\epsilon$ is an isomorphism $\Lambda^2 \mathbb{C}^2 \cong \mathbb{C}$.*

- *For $g \in G$, $\Lambda^2 g = \det(g) \cdot \mathrm{id}$, so $\epsilon$-preservation forces $\det(g) = 1$: this is why the gauge group is $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ rather than $\mathrm{GL}(2, \mathbb{C})$ or $\mathrm{U}(2)$.*

</div>

<div id="thm:su2-emergence" class="theorem">

**Theorem 2.9** (Emergence of the gauge group). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.RankOneGaugeData)*

*Let $(\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)$ be a ([quantum observable universe](#def:quantum-observable-universe)). Then $G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) \cong \mathrm{SU}(2)$ (or $\mathrm{SL}(2, R)$ depending on the signature of the Frobenius pairing).*

</div>

<div class="proof">

*Proof of Emergence of the gauge group.* <span id="prf:su2-emergence" label="prf:su2-emergence"></span>

The gauge group $G$ is defined via Tannaka–Krein duality as the group scheme of tensor-preserving natural automorphisms of the fibre functor $\tau$. An element $g \in G$ assigns an invertible linear map $g_X \colon \tau(X) \to \tau(X)$ to every object $X \in \mathbf{C}$.

Because $g$ is a natural transformation, it commutes with all morphisms in $\mathbf{C}$, including the volume constraint $\epsilon \colon \Lambda^2 V \to \mathbf{1}$ [volume constraint](#eq:categorical-volume-constraint). Applying $\tau$ yields the commutative diagram of $R$-modules

$$\label{eq:su2-emergence-diagram}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3.5em]
  \Lambda^2 \tau(V)
    \ar[r, "\Lambda^2 g_V"]
    \ar[d, "\tau(\epsilon)"']
  & \Lambda^2 \tau(V)
    \ar[d, "\tau(\epsilon)"]
  \\
  \tau(\mathbf{1})
    \ar[r, "g_{\mathbf{1}} = \mathrm{id}"']
  & \tau(\mathbf{1})
\end{tikzcd}$$

The volume constraint requires a non-degenerate epimorphism $\epsilon \colon \Lambda^2 V \to \mathbf{1}$, which forces $\mathrm{rank}(V) = 2$: the epimorphism is non-degenerate only when $\Lambda^2 V$ has rank $1$, and $\mathrm{rank}(\Lambda^2 V) = \binom{r}{2}$ equals $1$ precisely for $r = 2$ (see [Remark](#rem:fundamental-object-explication)). Thus $\tau(V)$ is a rank-$2$ free $R$-module and $\Lambda^2 \tau(V)$ has rank $1$. The induced operator $\Lambda^2 g_V$ acts on this rank-$1$ module as scalar multiplication by $\det(g_V)$. Following diagram [above](#eq:su2-emergence-diagram) from the top-left to the bottom-right:

$$\tau(\epsilon) \circ \Lambda^2 g_V
  =
  g_{\mathbf{1}} \circ \tau(\epsilon)
  =
  \tau(\epsilon).$$

Since $\tau(\epsilon)$ is non-degenerate (hence non-zero), this forces

$$\label{eq:det-one}
  \det(g_V) \;=\; 1,$$

restricting the natural automorphisms from $\mathrm{GL}(2)$ to the special subgroup $\mathrm{SL}(2)$.

The QOU non-degeneracy axiom ensures the Frobenius form $\int_A \colon A \to \mathbf{1}$ is non-degenerate, inducing the Frobenius self-duality $A \cong A^{\vee}$ ([fibre adjoint involution](#prop:fiber-adjoint-involution)). Define a dagger on morphisms by $f^{\dagger} = \int_A \circ \mu(S(f) \otimes -)$, where $S$ is the antipode. Non-degeneracy of $\int_A$ and faithfulness of $\tau$ imply $f^{\dagger} \circ f = 0 \Rightarrow f = 0$, so this is a positive-definite dagger structure ([positive definite dagger](#prop:positive-definite-dagger)). Every tensor automorphism $g \in G$ preserves the dagger (it commutes with $S$ and $\int_A$), forcing $g_V^{-1} = g_V^{\dagger}$ and restricting $G$ to the unitary subgroup $\mathrm{U}(2)$.

Combining both constraints:

$$G \;=\; \mathrm{SL}(2) \;\cap\; \mathrm{U}(2)
  \;=\; \mathrm{SU}(2).$$

The volume constraint provides the special-linear condition ($\det = 1$), while the positive-definite dagger structure provides the compactness (unitarity), locking the gauge group exclusively to $\mathrm{SU}(2)$. ◻

</div>

<div id="ex:su2-emergence" class="example">

**Example 2.10** (Emergence of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$: the full chain). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.Examples.su2Emergence)*

*Continuing [Examples](#ex:frobenius-su2)–[Example](#ex:dagger-su2), let $\mathbf{C} = \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2))$, $A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))$, $\tau$ the forgetful functor.*

1.  **Volume constraint* $\Rightarrow$ $\det(g_V) = 1$. The alternating form $\epsilon(v \wedge w) = v_1 w_2 - v_2 w_1$ on $V = \mathbb{C}^2$ is $\mathrm{SU}(2)$-invariant. Any tensor automorphism $g$ preserves $\epsilon$, forcing $g_V \in \mathrm{SL}(2, \mathbb{C})$.*

2.  **Dagger structure* $\Rightarrow$ unitarity. The dagger on $\mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2))$ ([dagger on SU(2)](#ex:dagger-su2)) forces $g_V^{-1} = g_V^{\dagger}$, cutting from $\mathrm{SL}(2, \mathbb{C})$ to its compact real form $\mathrm{SU}(2)$.*

3.  **Conclusion.* $G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) \cong \mathrm{SU}(2)$, recovering the input gauge group from the categorical axioms alone.*

</div>

<div id="rem:spin-half-representation" class="remark">

**Remark 2.11** (The spin-$\tfrac{1}{2}$ representation $V_{1/2}$).

*After [SU(2) emergence](#thm:su2-emergence) identifies $G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) \cong \mathrm{SU}(2)$, the abstract fundamental object $V$ acquires its concrete incarnation as the *spin-$\tfrac{1}{2}$ representation*:*

*$$V_{1/2} \;=\; \tau(V) \;\cong\; \mathbb{C}^2,$$*

*the defining two-dimensional representation of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$.*

*The [spin label](#prop:spin-labels) indexing $j \in \{0, \tfrac{1}{2}, 1, \tfrac{3}{2}, \ldots\}$ identifies each simple object $V_j$ with the unique irreducible representation of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ of dimension $2j+1$. In particular:*

- *$V_0 = \mathbf{1}$ (the trivial representation),*

- *$V_{1/2} = V \cong \mathbb{C}^2$ (the fundamental representation),*

- *$V_1 = \mathrm{Ad}(A) \cong \mathfrak{su}(2) \cong \mathbb{R}^3$ (the adjoint representation).*

*The standard basis $\{e_+, e_-\}$ of $V_{1/2}$ consists of weight vectors for the maximal torus $T \subset \mathrm{SU}(2)$:*

*$$T \cdot e_{\pm} \;=\; e^{\pm i\theta}\, e_{\pm},
  \qquad
  T = \left\{\!
    \begin{pmatrix} e^{i\theta} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{-i\theta} \end{pmatrix}
  \right\}.$$*

*The Clebsch–Gordan decomposition*

*$$V_{1/2} \otimes V_{1/2}
  \;\cong\;
  V_0 \;\oplus\; V_1$$*

*decomposes the tensor square into the singlet (antisymmetric, $\Lambda^2 V_{1/2}$) and the triplet (symmetric, $\mathrm{Sym}^2 V_{1/2}$). This is the simplest instance of [tensor generation](#rem:simple-objects-V): all $V_j$ arise as summands of $V_{1/2}^{\otimes 2j}$.*

</div>

## Maximal torus and weight decomposition

<div id="def:maximal-torus" class="definition">

**Definition 2.12** (Maximal torus and weight subcategory). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.MaximalTorus)*

*Let $(\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)$ be a ([quantum observable universe](#def:quantum-observable-universe)) with fundamental object $V$ (the unique simple object of categorical dimension $2$; see [spin labels](#prop:spin-labels) for the full labelling). The *weight subcategory* $\langle V \rangle \subset \mathbf{C}$ is the full subcategory whose objects are direct sums of weight spaces of $V$ (i.e. simultaneous eigenspaces of the Cartan subalgebra action). The *maximal torus* of the gauge group is*

*$$T = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau|_{\langle V \rangle}),$$*

*the sub-group scheme of $G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau)$ ([SU(2) emergence](#thm:su2-emergence)) consisting of those natural automorphisms that act diagonally on each weight space of $V$.*

*$$\label{eq:maximal-torus-diagram}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em]
  T \ar[r, hook] \ar[d, "\mathrm{diag}"']
  & G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) \ar[d] \\
  \mathrm{Aut}(\tau(V))
  & \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) \ar[l]
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad\text{(maximal torus)}$$*

*Equivalently, $T$ is the largest subgroup of $G$ for which every object in $\langle V \rangle$ decomposes into one-dimensional $T$-eigenspaces.*

</div>

<div id="ex:maximal-torus-su2" class="example">

**Example 2.13** (Maximal torus for $\mathrm{SU}(2)$). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.Examples.su2MaximalTorus)*

*Continuing [spin labels on SU(2)](#ex:spin-labels-su2), the fundamental object is $V = \mathbb{C}^2$ with the standard $\mathrm{SU}(2)$-action. The weight decomposition is $V = \mathbb{C} e_+ \oplus \mathbb{C} e_-$ (the $\pm\tfrac{1}{2}$-eigenspaces of $e_3 = \frac{1}{2}\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{smallmatrix}$). The weight subcategory $\langle V \rangle$ consists of representations that decompose into weight spaces: $V$ itself, $\mathbf{1}$, and their direct sums. The maximal torus is*

*$$T = \mathrm{U}(1)
  = \left\{
    \begin{pmatrix} e^{i\theta} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{-i\theta} \end{pmatrix}
    : \theta \in \mathbb{R}
  \right\},$$*

*the diagonal matrices in $\mathrm{SU}(2)$. Each element of $T$ acts on $e_{\pm}$ by $e^{\pm i\theta}$: one-dimensional eigenspaces, as required.*

</div>

<div id="def:weight-decomposition" class="definition">

**Definition 2.14** (Weight decomposition). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.WeightDecomposition)*

*Let $(\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)$ be a ([quantum observable universe](#def:quantum-observable-universe)) with maximal torus $T$ ([maximal torus](#def:maximal-torus)) and higher differential forms $\Omega^k(A)$ ([higher forms](#def:higher-forms)). The $T$-action on $\Omega^k(A)$ induces a $\mathbb{Z}$-grading by weights. Denoting by $\pi_H, \pi_V$ the projections onto the weight-$0$ and non-zero-weight summands, every $\alpha \in \Omega^k(A)$ decomposes uniquely:*

*$$\label{eq:weight-decomposition-cd}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2em, column sep=3em]
  & \Omega^k(A) \ar[dl, "\pi_H"'] \ar[dr, "\pi_V"] & \\
  \Omega^k_H(A) \ar[rr, hook, "\oplus"']
  & & \Omega^k_V(A)
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad \alpha = \alpha_H + \alpha_V.$$*

*Here $\alpha_H = \pi_H(\alpha)$ is the *horizontal component* (weight-$0$ under $T$) and $\alpha_V = \pi_V(\alpha)$ is the *vertical component* (non-zero weight). A form is *purely horizontal* if and only if $\alpha_V = 0$.*

</div>

<div id="thm:weight-decomposition-exists" class="theorem">

**Theorem 2.15** (Existence of the weight decomposition). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.WeightDecomposition.ofMaximalTorus)*

*Let $(\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)$ be a ([quantum observable universe](#def:quantum-observable-universe)) with [maximal torus](#def:maximal-torus) $T$ acting on [higher forms](#def:higher-forms) $\Omega^k(A)$. Then there exists a [weight decomposition](#def:weight-decomposition) $(\pi_H, \pi_V)$ of $\Omega^k(A)$ satisfying:*

1.  ***Complementarity:** $\pi_H + \pi_V = \mathrm{id}$.*

2.  ***Idempotency:** $\pi_H^2 = \pi_H$ and $\pi_V^2 = \pi_V$.*

*$$\label{eq:weight-decomposition-exists-diagram}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em]
  \Omega^k(A) \ar[r, "\pi_H"] \ar[d, "\pi_V"']
  & \Omega^k_H(A) \\
  \Omega^k_V(A)
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad (\pi_H + \pi_V = \mathrm{id},\; \pi_H \pi_V = 0)$$*

</div>

<div class="proof">

*Proof of existence of the weight decomposition.* <span id="prf:weight-decomposition-exists" label="prf:weight-decomposition-exists"></span>

The projections are constructed from the torus averaging operator: for each weight $\lambda$ of the $T$-action, the $\lambda$-isotypic projector $e_\lambda$ is idempotent, and $\pi_H = e_0$, $\pi_V = \mathrm{id} - e_0$. ◻

</div>

## Vectors, hadrons, and the PawLei basis

<div id="rem:adjoint-trace" class="remark">

**Remark 2.16** (Adjoint trace and the categorical inner product).

*The [Frobenius pairing](#def:frobenius-pairing) and the [fibre-adjoint involution](#prop:fiber-adjoint-involution) together equip every hom-space $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}(X, Y)$ with a canonical sesquilinear form. Define the *adjoint trace* on endomorphisms of $V$ by*

*$$\mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Ad}}(f)
  \;=\;
  \int_A \!\circ\; \mu \circ (f \otimes \mathrm{id}_{V^{\vee}})
    \circ \mathrm{coev}_V
  \;\in\;
  \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{1}) \cong R,$$*

*where $\mathrm{coev}_V \colon \mathbf{1} \to V \otimes V^{\vee}$ is the coevaluation (from rigidity) and $\mu$ is the Frobenius multiplication on $A$.*

*This trace has two key properties:*

1.  ***Cyclicity**: $\mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Ad}}(f \circ g) = \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Ad}}(g \circ f)$, inherited from the Frobenius relation.*

2.  ***Non-degeneracy**: the induced pairing $\langle f, g \rangle_{\mathrm{Ad}} = \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Ad}}(f^{\dagger} \circ g)$ is non-degenerate, because $\int_A$ is non-degenerate and the dagger is positive-definite.*

*In the archimedean realisation with $G = \mathrm{SU}(2)$, the adjoint trace recovers the Killing form on $\mathfrak{su}(2)$:*

*$$\mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Ad}}(f)
  \;=\;
  \mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{ad}(f))
  \;=\;
  -2\,\mathrm{tr}_{\mathbb{C}^2}(f).$$*

</div>

<div id="prop:pawlowski-leitner-basis" class="proposition">

**Proposition 2.17** (Pawlowski–Leitner basis for $\mathrm{Hom}(V_j, V_{1/2}^{\otimes n})$). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.PawLeiBasis)*

*Let $G = \mathrm{SU}(2)$ be the emergent gauge group ([SU(2) emergence](#thm:su2-emergence)) and let $V_{1/2} \cong \mathbb{C}^2$ be the [spin-$\tfrac{1}{2}$ representation](#rem:spin-half-representation). For each simple object $V_j$ and tensor power $V_{1/2}^{\otimes n}$ with $n \geq 2j$, the intertwiner space*

*$$\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{SU}(2)}\!\bigl(V_j,\;
    V_{1/2}^{\otimes n}\bigr)$$*

*admits a *canonical* basis — the **PawLei basis** — indexed by standard Young tableaux of shape $\lambda \vdash n$ with at most $2$ rows and with $\lambda_1 - \lambda_2 = 2j$.*

*The construction rests on the [PBW theorem over commutative rings](#cor:pbw): the unital Gröbner basis for $U(\mathfrak{su}(2))$ provides a monomial basis for the enveloping algebra, from which the intertwiner basis is derived by contraction with the volume form.*

*$$\label{eq:pawlei-basis-diagram}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em]
  \mathbf{1} \ar[r, "\epsilon^{\vee}"]
  & \Lambda^2 V_{1/2} \ar[r, hook]
  & V_{1/2}^{\otimes n} \ar[r, "\pi_j"]
  & V_j
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad\text{(PawLei contraction)}$$*

*Concretely, the volume form $\epsilon \colon \Lambda^2 V_{1/2} \to \mathbf{1}$ and its dual $\epsilon^{\vee} \colon \mathbf{1} \to \Lambda^2 V_{1/2}$ generate *contraction operators* on tensor powers. The PawLei basis elements are obtained by applying a specific sequence of pairwise contractions (determined by the tableau) to the highest-weight vector $e_+^{\otimes (j+m)} \otimes e_-^{\otimes (j-m)}$, then symmetrising according to the row structure of the tableau.*

*The dimension of the intertwiner space is given by the hook-length formula:*

*$$\dim\,\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{SU}(2)}\!\bigl(V_j,\;
    V_{1/2}^{\otimes n}\bigr)
  \;=\;
  \frac{(2j+1)\, n!}{(\tfrac{n}{2}+j+1)!\;(\tfrac{n}{2}-j)!}$$*

*when $n \equiv 2j \pmod{2}$, and zero otherwise.*

*The PBW basis underlying this construction is established via unital Gröbner bases in \\}cite{leitnerpawloski2004}.*

</div>

<div id="prop:pawlowski-leitner-inner-product" class="proposition">

**Proposition 2.18** (Inner product on intertwiner spaces). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.PawLeiInnerProduct)*

*The [adjoint trace](#rem:adjoint-trace) induces a canonical inner product on intertwiner spaces. For $\phi, \psi \in \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{SU}(2)}(V_j,\, V_{1/2}^{\otimes n})$, define*

*$$\langle \phi, \psi \rangle_{\mathrm{PL}}
  \;=\;
  \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Ad}}\!\bigl(\phi^{\dagger} \circ \psi\bigr)
  \;=\;
  \int_A \!\circ\; \mu \circ
    (\phi^{\dagger} \circ \psi \otimes \mathrm{id})
    \circ \mathrm{coev}_{V_j}.$$*

*$$\label{eq:pawlei-inner-product-diagram}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em]
  \mathbf{1} \ar[r, "\mathrm{coev}_{V_j}"]
  & V_j \otimes V_j^{\vee}
    \ar[r, "\phi^{\dagger} \circ \psi \,\otimes\, \mathrm{id}"]
  & A \otimes V_j^{\vee}
    \ar[r, "\int_A \circ \mu"]
  & \mathbf{1}
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad\text{(PawLei inner product)}$$*

*The [PawLei basis](#prop:pawlowski-leitner-basis) $\{T_{\lambda}\}$ is *orthogonal* with respect to this pairing:*

*$$\langle T_{\lambda}, T_{\mu} \rangle_{\mathrm{PL}}
