***Statement.** For any knot composite $\mathfrak{H}$ with crossing energy $\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(\mathfrak{H}) = \sum_i \epsilon_i$ where $\epsilon_i \in \{q, -q^{-1}\}$:*

1.  ***Symmetric channel.** The component $E_{\mathrm{sym}}(\mathfrak{H}) = \sum_i |\epsilon_i| \cdot \cosh(\ln q) \cdot \mathrm{sgn}(\epsilon_i)$ is invariant under the mirror operation $\sigma$ (which reverses all crossing signs).*

2.  ***Antisymmetric channel.** The component $E_{\mathrm{asym}}(\mathfrak{H}) = \sum_i |\epsilon_i| \cdot \sinh(\ln q) \cdot \mathrm{sgn}(\epsilon_i)$ reverses sign under $\sigma$.*

3.  ***Pair cancellation.** For a particle–antiparticle pair $(\mathfrak{H}, \mathfrak{H}^{\sigma})$, the combined crossing energy is purely antisymmetric: $$\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(\mathfrak{H}) + \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(\mathfrak{H}^{\sigma})
      \;=\; 2\,E_{\mathrm{asym}}(\mathfrak{H}).$$*

4.  ***Ratio identity.** The antisymmetric-to-symmetric ratio is $$\frac{E_{\mathrm{asym}}}{E_{\mathrm{sym}}}
      \;=\; \tanh(\ln q),$$ independent of the knot composite $\mathfrak{H}$.*

</div>

<div id="rem:virtual-particles-exceptional-divisor" class="remark">

**Remark 10.27** (Virtual particles as excitations of the exceptional divisor).

*In quantum field theory, virtual particles are internal lines in Feynman diagrams: off-shell excitations that mediate forces and contribute to loop corrections but are never directly detected. Their "existence" is bounded by the Heisenberg uncertainty relation $\Delta E \cdot \Delta t \gtrsim \hbar$. The QOU framework provides a geometric home for this phenomenon.*

***The exceptional divisor as the virtual stage.***

*At each brane point $p \in M$, the blow-up replaces $p$ with an [exceptional divisor](#def:exceptional-divisor) $\mathcal{S}_p \cong \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C}) \cong S^2$. This sphere parametrises the *directions* of departure from the base manifold — the internal degrees of freedom invisible to the base-level observer.*

*A virtual particle is an excitation that lives **within** the Reeb bundle over $\mathcal{S}_p$ — the Hopf fibration $U(1) \hookrightarrow S^3 \to \mathcal{S}_p$ where all braiding takes place ([vertex is the exceptional divisor](#prop:vertex-is-exceptional-divisor)). It is created at the blow-up locus, propagates along the exceptional divisor (or up into the [brane tower](#def:recursive-brane-tower) rooted at $\mathcal{S}_p$), and is reabsorbed before it can descend to the base level $A_0$.*

***Brane tower levels as virtual depth.***

*The [recursive brane tower](#def:recursive-brane-tower) $A_0 \hookrightarrow A_1 \hookrightarrow A_2 \hookrightarrow \cdots$ stratifies excitations by their [jet prolongation](#prop:jet-prolongation) level. Physical (on-shell) particles live at level $A_0$ — they are knot configurations in the base algebra. Virtual particles live at levels $A_n$ with $n \geq 1$:*

| *Tower level*      | *Algebra*                                       | *Physical interpretation*                           |
|:-------------------|:------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------|
| *$A_0 = A$*        | *Coordinate ring $\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))$* | *On-shell particles: knots in base manifold*        |
| *$A_1 = J^1(A_0)$* | *Sections of frame bundle*                      | *1-virtual: connection fluctuations (gauge bosons)* |
| *$A_2 = J^1(A_1)$* | *Second jet sections*                           | *2-virtual: curvature fluctuations (graviton-like)* |
| *$A_n$*            | *$n$-th jet sections*                           | *$n$-virtual: $n$-th derivative corrections*        |

*Each level $A_n$ has dimension $3^n \cdot \dim A_0$ (for $\mathrm{SU}(2)$), so the state space grows exponentially with virtual depth — but the projection back to $A_0$ collapses all higher-level structure.*

***Why virtual particles are never observed.***

*An excitation at level $A_n$ ($n \geq 1$) is invisible at $A_0$ because the canonical projection $\pi_0 \colon A_n \to A_0$ annihilates the $\Omega^1$ components:*

*$$\pi_0(f \otimes \omega_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes \omega_n)
  \;=\;
  f \cdot \varepsilon(\omega_1) \cdots \varepsilon(\omega_n),$$*

*where $\varepsilon$ is the counit. For a form $\omega$ with no constant part ($\varepsilon(\omega) = 0$), the entire excitation projects to zero at the base level. The virtual particle exists in the tower but casts no shadow on $A_0$.*

*This is the categorical analogue of the statement that virtual particles are "off-shell": they satisfy the equations of motion at their tower level but not at the base level. The base-level observer sees only the *net effect* — a correction to the propagator, an effective force, a shift in energy levels — never the virtual excitation itself.*

***Lifetime from the Heisenberg commutator.***

*The [Heisenberg commutator](#rem:heisenberg-commutator) at level $n$ of the tower is*

*$$[\hat{X}, \hat{P}]_{q_n} \;=\; J\,\hbar_{q_n}, \qquad
  \hbar_{q_n} \;=\; 1 - q_n^{-1},$$*

*where $q_n$ is the substrate parameter at the $n$-th level. The uncertainty bound $\Delta E \cdot \Delta t \geq \hbar_{q_n} / 2$ limits the lifetime of a virtual excitation at level $n$:*

*$$\Delta t_{\text{virtual}}
  \;\leq\;
  \frac{\hbar_{q_n}}{2\,\Delta E}.$$*

*For an excitation that borrows energy $\Delta E$ from the vacuum at the exceptional divisor, this is the maximum time before the excitation must be reabsorbed. Crucially, the excitation’s "worldline" stays within the tower: it is created at $\mathcal{S}_p$, propagates through $A_1, A_2, \ldots$, and returns to $\mathcal{S}_p$ without ever descending to $A_0$.*

</div>

**What is CP violation?** CP symmetry is the combined operation of charge conjugation C (swap particle $\leftrightarrow$ antiparticle) and parity P (mirror spatial coordinates). If physics were CP-symmetric, matter and antimatter would behave as exact mirror images. **CP violation** means this symmetry is broken: certain processes distinguish matter from antimatter at a fundamental level.

**Experimental evidence.**

CP violation is firmly established in three systems:

1.  **Neutral kaons** (1964). Cronin and Fitch observed that the long-lived kaon $K_L$ (which should decay only to three pions under CP symmetry) occasionally decays to two pions: $K_L \to \pi^+\pi^-$ at rate $\sim 2 \times 10^{-3}$ \\}cite{christenson1964}. This was the first evidence that CP is not an exact symmetry.

2.  **$B$ mesons** (2001). The BaBar \\}cite{aubert2001} and Belle experiments measured CP-violating asymmetries in $B^0 \to J/\psi\,K_S$ decays, confirming the Kobayashi–Maskawa mechanism: the CKM quark-mixing matrix contains an irreducible complex phase $\delta_{\mathrm{CKM}}$ that cannot be removed by field redefinitions.

3.  **$D$ mesons** (2019). LHCb observed CP violation in charm decays ($D^0 \to K^+K^-$ vs $D^0 \to \pi^+\pi^-$) at the $10^{-4}$ level.

**The matter–antimatter asymmetry.**

Sakharov (1967) showed that three conditions are necessary for the observed baryon asymmetry of the universe: (i) baryon number violation, (ii) C and CP violation, (iii) departure from thermal equilibrium. The Standard Model CKM phase provides (ii) but is quantitatively too small by several orders of magnitude to explain the observed ratio $n_B / n_\gamma \sim 6 \times 10^{-10}$. Additional sources of CP violation are needed.

**QOU interpretation.**

In the [complex chirality rotation](#conj:complex-chirality-rotation) framework, CP violation arises from a residual phase $\theta$ of the complex substrate parameter $q = |q|\,e^{i\theta}$:

- The observable sector projects $\theta \to 0$, but this projection may be imperfect — a small residual $\theta_{\mathrm{res}}$ could survive.

- The CP-violating discriminant is $\delta_{\mathrm{CP}} \sim \mathcal{O}(\theta_{\mathrm{res}}^2)$ for single-crossing systems (electron/positron).

- For **multi-crossing composites** (kaons: quark–antiquark with multiple internal crossings), the phase accumulates: $\delta_{\mathrm{CP}} \sim n_c\,\theta_{\mathrm{res}}$, where $n_c$ is the total crossing number of the hadronic braid word.

- This provides a **geometric origin** for the CKM phase: it is the total accumulated crossing phase from the complex-$q$ sector, projected onto the observable quark-mixing matrix.

**Quantitative gap.** The [crossing energy decomposition](#rem:crossing-energy-decomposition) gives the electromagnetic/strong ratio $\tanh(\ln q) \approx 0.104$. If the residual phase scales similarly — $\theta_{\mathrm{res}} \sim \tanh(\ln q) \cdot \alpha_{\mathrm{EM}}$ — then $\delta_{\mathrm{CP}} \sim 10^{-3}$, which is the right order of magnitude for kaon CP violation but still too small for baryogenesis. The missing enhancement may come from the **cosmological regime** where the observability constraint itself weakens.

<div id="rem:electron-immortality" class="remark">

**Remark 10.28** (Electrons are immortal: no beta decay for elementary trefoils).

*Beta decay converts a neutron to a proton (or vice versa) by changing the crossing orientation partition of the [Borromean baryon](#def:borromean-baryon): $[u,d,d] \to [u,u,d]$. This is possible because baryons are **composite** — they have internal degrees of freedom (the quark flavour assignments) that can rearrange via R-I embedding moves while preserving the Borromean link type.*

***Can the electron beta-decay?***

*No — and the reason is topological, not energetic. The electron is the trefoil $T_{2,3}$: an **elementary** knot with no internal constituents. There is no crossing orientation partition to rearrange, no substructure to reorganise, no embedding move that changes the particle’s identity. The electron has exactly one degree of freedom — its knot type — and that is a topological invariant.*

| *Particle* | *Structure*                         | *Internal d.o.f.*         | *Beta decay?*                                                  |
|:-----------|:------------------------------------|:--------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------|
| *Neutron*  | *$[u,d,d]_p \bowtie \mathcal{L}_H$* | *Quark flavour partition* | *Yes: $\mathfrak{n} \to \mathfrak{p} + e^- + \nu^{\sigma}$*    |
| *Proton*   | *$[u,u,d]_p \bowtie \mathcal{L}_H$* | *Quark flavour partition* | *Yes (in nuclei): $\mathfrak{p} \to \mathfrak{n} + e^+ + \nu$* |
| *Electron* | *$T_{2,3}$*                         | *None*                    | ***No***                                                       |
| *Neutrino* | *$T_{1,0}$ (unknot)*                | *None*                    | ***No***                                                       |

*The electron cannot decay into anything lighter while conserving lepton number and charge. There is no lighter charged lepton, and the neutrino (unknot $T_{1,0}$) has zero crossing energy and zero mass — it cannot absorb the electron’s topological charge.*

***Electrons survive to heat death.***

*In the observable era ($1 < q < \infty$), the [time reversal barrier](#rem:time-reversal-energy-barrier) prevents chirality reversal, and the absence of beta decay prevents flavour change. The electron is therefore **immortal** in the observable sector: it persists from the moment of its creation (pair production at the exceptional divisor) until the cosmological boundary.*

*As the universe evolves toward heat death ($q \to 1$):*

1.  ***Bound electrons** are liberated. Atoms ionise as the ambient energy drops below binding thresholds — but the *electron itself* is unchanged. Its bare mass (a knot invariant) is eternal; only its binding energy (an embedding property) dissipates.*

2.  ***Free electrons become radiation.** In the $q \to 1$ limit, the crossing energy asymmetry $q - q^{-1} \to 0$ erases the Coulomb distinction. The electron’s electromagnetic charge effectively vanishes. What remains is a massless topological excitation — indistinguishable from a photon in the frozen geometry.*

3.  ***Radiation becomes CMB.** The thermal photon bath (including the absorbed electron contribution) redshifts to the cosmic microwave background. The [CMB torsion signature](#rem:cmb-q-torsion) carries the imprint of the $q$-deformed Reeb flow — a fossil record of the substrate parameter’s value during earlier epochs.*

***Into the next aeon.***

*If the [cosmological chirality flip](#rem:cosmological-chirality-flip) is correct, the heat-death boundary is where chirality distinction collapses ($q \to 1$) and the next aeon’s big bang is where it re-emerges ($q \to \infty$ in the new cycle). The CMB radiation from one aeon becomes the initial condition for the next — carrying topological information (knot type) through the boundary even as metric information (mass, charge) is erased.*

*In the language of Penrose’s Conformal Cyclic Cosmology: the massless, chargeless radiation at heat death is conformally equivalent to the initial singularity of the next aeon. In the QOU framework, this equivalence is not conformal rescaling but **Frobenius degeneration**: the same mathematical structure (the Frobenius form becoming trivial or singular) governs both endpoints, and the exceptional divisors at the boundary are where the topology resets.*

*The electron, as a trefoil, is (k)not subject to beta decay. It lives forever — or rather, it lives until the concept of "living" loses meaning at $q = 1$, where all distinctions dissolve into the frozen geometry of the classical limit.*

</div>

## Organic Chemistry from Hopf Chains

<div id="def:covalent-bond-types" class="definition">

**Definition 10.29** (Covalent bond (shared Hopf links)). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.Organic.CovalentBond)*

*Metallic bonding ([metallic character](#prop:metallic-character-knot)) arises when residual sub-links are shared across a lattice. **Covalent bonding** is the molecular version: two atoms share a small, fixed number of trefoils between their residual sub-links, forming a **localised** shared Hopf link rather than a lattice-spanning delocalised chain.*

***Definition.** Let $\mathcal{A}_1$ and $\mathcal{A}_2$ be atoms with residual sub-links $R_1$ and $R_2$. A **covalent bond** of order $k$ is a shared sub-Hopf link*

*$$B_k(R_1, R_2)
  \;=\;
  \underbrace{T_{2,3} \bowtie \cdots \bowtie T_{2,3}}_{k \text{ shared trefoils}}$$*

*where each shared trefoil is simultaneously Hopf-linked to one open site in $R_1$ and one open site in $R_2$. The integer $k$ is the **bond order**:*

| *Bond order $k$* | *Chemical name* | *Shared trefoils* | *Linking sites consumed* |
|:----------------:|:----------------|:-----------------:|:------------------------:|
|       *1*        | *Single bond*   |        *1*        |       *1 per atom*       |
|       *2*        | *Double bond*   |        *2*        |       *2 per atom*       |
|       *3*        | *Triple bond*   |        *3*        |       *3 per atom*       |

*The crossing energy of the bond is*

*$$E_{\mathrm{bond}}(k)
  \;=\;
  k \cdot \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(T(2,2))
  \;+\;
  \binom{k}{2} \, \Delta E_{\mathrm{inter}},$$*

*where $T(2,2)$ is the Hopf link ([crossing energy](#def:crossing-energy)), the first term accounts for $k$ individual Hopf links, and the second for inter-link interactions within the shared sub-link. Higher bond order increases both binding strength and rigidity: a triple bond is both stronger and stiffer than a single bond because the three shared trefoils form a closed sub-link that resists Reidemeister moves.*

</div>

<div id="def:molecular-hopf-chain" class="definition">

**Definition 10.30** (Molecular Hopf chain (open)). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.Organic.MolecularHopfChain)*

*A **molecular Hopf chain** is a linear sequence of atoms bonded by covalent Hopf links ([covalent bond](#def:covalent-bond-types)), where the first and last atoms retain unused linking sites.*

***Definition.** Let $\mathcal{A}_1, \ldots, \mathcal{A}_N$ be atoms with residual sub-links $R_1, \ldots, R_N$. A **molecular Hopf chain** of length $N$ and bond order $k$ is the composite*

*$$\mathcal{C}_N^{(k)}
  \;=\;
  \mathcal{A}_1
  \;\underset{B_k}{\bowtie}\;
  \mathcal{A}_2
  \;\underset{B_k}{\bowtie}\;
  \cdots
  \;\underset{B_k}{\bowtie}\;
  \mathcal{A}_N$$*

*where $B_k(R_i, R_{i+1})$ is a covalent bond of order $k$ between adjacent atoms. The **linking matrix** of the chain is the $N \times N$ matrix*

*$$L^{\mathrm{chain}}_{ij}
  \;=\;
  \begin{cases}
    k & \text{if } |i - j| = 1, \\
    0 & \text{otherwise}.
  \end{cases}$$*

*This is a **tridiagonal** matrix — each atom is linked only to its immediate neighbours.*

***Boundary conditions.** The endpoint atoms $\mathcal{A}_1$ and $\mathcal{A}_N$ each consume only $k$ of their available linking sites for the chain bond. The remaining open sites are **free endpoints**: they can bond to hydrogen, to side chains, or remain as dangling links. For a homoatomic chain of carbon atoms ($k = 1$), each interior carbon uses 2 of its 4 sites for the chain backbone, leaving 2 for side bonds; each endpoint carbon uses 1, leaving 3.*

***Crossing energy of the chain.** The total crossing energy is the sum over $N - 1$ bonds:*

*$$\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(\mathcal{C}_N^{(k)})
  \;=\;
  (N - 1) \cdot E_{\mathrm{bond}}(k).$$*

*The absence of a bond between $\mathcal{A}_1$ and $\mathcal{A}_N$ — the **missing link** — is the defining feature distinguishing chains from rings.*

</div>

<div id="def:threading-link" class="definition">

**Definition 10.31** (Threading link $T(2,N)$). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.Organic.ThreadingLink)*

*A **threading link** is a single torus link that passes through all atoms in a molecular ring simultaneously, replacing the pairwise Hopf link picture with a non-local, correlated binding structure.*

***Definition.** Let $\mathcal{A}_1, \ldots, \mathcal{A}_N$ be atoms arranged in a cycle. The **threading link** of the ring is the torus link*

*$$\mathcal{T}_N \;=\; T(2, N),$$*

*whose closure in the braid group $B_N$ is*

*$$\hat{\beta}_N
  \;=\;
  (\sigma_1 \, \sigma_2 \, \cdots \, \sigma_{N-1})^2.$$*

*The threading link winds **twice** around the torus defined by the $N$ atoms, passing through every atom on each winding. It has $2(N-1)$ crossings in the standard braid representation — all of the same sign.*

***Component structure.** The number of components of $T(2,N)$ is $\gcd(2,N)$:*

| *$N$*  | *$\gcd(2,N)$* | *Components* | *Each component*                        |
|:------:|:-------------:|:------------:|:----------------------------------------|
| *odd*  |      *1*      |  *1 (knot)*  | *$T(1, N)$ — unknot wrapping $N$ times* |
| *even* |      *2*      |  *2 (link)*  | *each unknotted, wrapping $N/2$ times*  |

*For even $N$ (the case of benzene, $N = 6$), the threading link is a **2-component link**: two unknotted loops, each threading through all $N$ atoms. These two components are the topological realisation of the two delocalised $\pi$ electrons.*

***Alexander polynomial.** The Alexander polynomial of $T(2,N)$ for even $N = 2m$ is*

*$$\Delta_{T(2,2m)}(t)
  \;=\;
  \frac{t^m - t^{-m}}{t - t^{-1}}.$$*

*Evaluated at the substrate parameter $t = q$:*

| *Threading*       | *$m$* | *$\Delta(q)$*                 |
|:------------------|:-----:|:------------------------------|
| *$T(2,2)$ (Hopf)* |  *1*  | *$1$*                         |
| *$T(2,4)$*        |  *2*  | *$q + q^{-1}$*                |
| *$T(2,6)$*        |  *3*  | *$q^2 + 1 + q^{-2}$*          |
| *$T(2,8)$*        |  *4*  | *$q^3 + q + q^{-1} + q^{-3}$* |

***Key identity.** For $T(2,6)$:*

*$$\Delta_{T(2,6)}(q)
  \;=\;
  q^2 + 1 + q^{-2}
  \;=\;
  (q + q^{-1})^2 - 1.$$*

*The threading link’s Alexander weight is **one less than the square** of the Hopf link energy quantum $|q + q^{-1}|$. This quadratic relation encodes the non-local correlation: the threading link "knows" about the Hopf link, but carries strictly less weight.*

***Contrast with pairwise Hopf links.** The pairwise picture bonds $N$ atoms with $N$ separate Hopf links, giving total Alexander weight $N \cdot \Delta_{T(2,2)}(q) = N$. The threading link replaces all $N$ bonds with a single invariant:*

*$$\frac{\Delta_{T(2,2m)}(q)}{N}
  \;=\;
  \frac{q^2 + 1 + q^{-2}}{6}
  \;\approx\;
  \frac{1}{2}
  \qquad (|q| \approx 1).$$*

*The threading carries **half the Alexander weight** of the pairwise construction. This factor of $\tfrac{1}{2}$ propagates directly into the crossing energy, halving the predicted ring-closure barrier.*

</div>

<div id="def:molecular-hopf-ring" class="definition">

**Definition 10.32** (Molecular Hopf ring (closed)). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.Organic.MolecularHopfRing)*

*A **molecular Hopf ring** is not a chain with its ends joined — it is a fundamentally different topological object. Where the chain bonds atoms pairwise via Hopf links ([molecular Hopf chain](#def:molecular-hopf-chain)), the ring binds all atoms simultaneously via a single **threading link** ([threading link](#def:threading-link)).*

***Definition.** Let $\mathcal{A}_1, \ldots, \mathcal{A}_N$ be atoms arranged in a cycle. A **molecular Hopf ring** of length $N$ is the composite*

*$$\mathcal{R}_N
  \;=\;
  [\mathcal{A}_1, \ldots, \mathcal{A}_N]
  \;\bowtie\;
  \mathcal{T}_N,$$*

*where $\mathcal{T}_N = T(2, N)$ is the threading link — a single torus link that passes through all $N$ atoms. The threading link’s braid word in $B_N$ is*

*$$\hat{\beta}_N
  \;=\;
  (\sigma_1 \, \sigma_2 \, \cdots \, \sigma_{N-1})^2,$$*

*with $2(N-1)$ crossings, all of the same sign.*

***Crossing energy of the ring.** The crossing energy is determined by the threading link’s Alexander polynomial evaluated at the substrate parameter:*

*$$\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(\mathcal{R}_N)
  \;\propto\;
  \Delta_{T(2,N)}(q).$$*

*For even $N = 2m$:*

*$$\Delta_{T(2,2m)}(q)
  \;=\;
  \frac{q^m - q^{-m}}{q - q^{-1}}.$$*

***Contrast with the pairwise picture.** A naïve ring built from $N$ separate Hopf links would have crossing energy proportional to $N \cdot \Delta_{T(2,2)}(q) = N$. The threading link replaces this with a single polynomial that evaluates to roughly $N/2$ — the threading is **topologically more efficient** than pairwise bonding.*

| *Structure*                 | *Binding*   |         *Alexander weight*         |      *Crossings*       |
|:----------------------------|:------------|:----------------------------------:|:----------------------:|
| *Chain ($N-1$ Hopf links)*  | *pairwise*  |             *$N - 1$*              |       *$2(N-1)$*       |
| *Ring ($N$ Hopf links)*     | *pairwise*  |               *$N$*                | *$2N$ + rearrangement* |
| *Ring ($T(2,N)$ threading)* | *non-local* | *$\Delta_{T(2,N)}(q) \approx N/2$* |       *$2(N-1)$*       |

*The threading ring has **fewer crossings than the pairwise ring** and **no rearrangement cost** — the threading link already connects all strands.*

***Rigidity.** The threading link passes through every atom twice (once per winding). Deforming the ring requires moving the threading link through all $N$ atoms simultaneously — a global operation. This is the topological origin of ring rigidity: it is not that individual bonds are stiff, but that the threading link correlates all atoms non-locally.*

</div>

<div id="prop:ring-closure-barrier" class="proposition">

**Proposition 10.33** (Ring-closure energy barrier from braid rearrangement). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.Organic.alexanderWeightDifference)*

*Closing a molecular Hopf chain into a ring is a **topological phase transition**: the pairwise Hopf link structure is replaced by a single threading link $T(2,N)$ ([threading link](#def:threading-link)). The energy barrier arises not from adding one more bond, but from reorganising the entire binding topology.*

***Statement.** Let $\mathcal{C}_N$ be a molecular Hopf chain of length $N$ ([molecular Hopf chain](#def:molecular-hopf-chain)), and let $\mathcal{R}_N$ be the corresponding threaded ring ([molecular Hopf ring](#def:molecular-hopf-ring)). The crossing energies, measured by Alexander polynomial evaluation at the substrate parameter $q$, are:*

*$$\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(\mathcal{C}_N)
  \;\propto\;
  (N-1) \cdot \Delta_{T(2,2)}(q)
  \;=\;
  N - 1,$$*

*$$\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(\mathcal{R}_N)
  \;\propto\;
  \Delta_{T(2,N)}(q)
  \;=\;
  \frac{q^{N/2} - q^{-N/2}}{q - q^{-1}}
  \quad (\text{for even } N).$$*

*For $N = 6$:*

*$$\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(\mathcal{C}_6)
  \;\propto\; 5,
  \qquad
  \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(\mathcal{R}_6)
  \;\propto\;
  q^2 + 1 + q^{-2}
  \;\approx\; 3
  \quad (|q| \approx 1).$$*

*The ring has **lower crossing energy** than the chain. It binds 6 atoms with Alexander weight $\approx 3$, compared to the chain’s weight of $5$ for only 5 pairwise bonds.*

***The barrier: topological reorganisation.** Despite the ring being energetically favourable, the transition $\mathcal{C}_N \to \mathcal{R}_N$ requires a discontinuous change in topology: $N - 1$ separate Hopf links must be **replaced** by a single threading link $T(2,N)$. This is not a continuous deformation — the braid word changes from a product of non-adjacent generators $\sigma_i^2$ to the correlated product $(\sigma_1 \cdots \sigma_{N-1})^2$.*

*The transition state is the configuration where the chain’s pairwise links are partially dissolved but the threading link has not yet formed. At this point, some bonds are broken but no threading stabilisation has been gained — the crossing energy is at a **maximum**:*

*$$\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(\text{transition})
  \;>\;
  \max\bigl(
    \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(\mathcal{C}_N),\;
    \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(\mathcal{R}_N)
  \bigr).$$*

*The activation barrier is the energy required to reach this intermediate state.*

***Ring super-stability from threading.** Once the threading link $T(2,N)$ forms, it locks the ring in a deep topological trap. Breaking the ring requires not just severing one bond but **dissolving the threading link entirely** — converting the correlated $T(2,N)$ back into $N$ separate Hopf links. The energy cost of ring-opening is:*

*$$\Delta E_{\mathrm{open}}
  \;=\;
  (N - 1) - \Delta_{T(2,N)}(q)
  \;+\;
  E_{\mathrm{activation}}.$$*

*For $N = 6$: the threading provides $5 - 3 = 2$ units of additional stabilisation beyond the pairwise picture, plus the full activation barrier must be re-climbed. The ring is super-stable because the threading link is a **lower-energy encoding** of the same binding — reverting to the pairwise encoding costs energy.*

***The spring analogy.** The open chain is a spring held apart. The threading link is what happens when the spring snaps shut: the separate coils (pairwise Hopf links) merge into a single, tighter winding ($T(2,N)$). The merged winding is more efficient (lower Alexander weight) and cannot be separated without unwinding the entire structure.*

</div>

<div id="prop:chain-ring-comparison" class="proposition">

**Proposition 10.34** (Predicted vs. observed $\mathrm{C}_6$ ring-closure barrier). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.Organic.benzene_weights)*

*The threading link picture makes a quantitative prediction — with **no free parameters** — that can be compared to experimental data.*

***Derivation chain.** Every quantity is determined by the Bring’s surface geometry:*

*$$\chi(A) = -6
  \;\xrightarrow{\text{Bring's surface}}\;
  \mathcal{G}
  \;\xrightarrow{\text{knot spectrum}}\;
  q,\; \alpha,\; m_e/m_p
  \;\xrightarrow{\text{scale separation}}\;
  |q + q^{-1}|_{\mathrm{mol}}
  \;\xrightarrow{\Delta_{T(2,6)}(q)}\;
  \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}.$$*

1.  *The substrate parameter $q$ is fixed by $\chi(A) = -6$ ([substrate parameter](#def:substrate-parameter)).*

2.  *The nuclear crossing energy quantum $|q + q^{-1}|_{\mathrm{nuc}} \sim 8\,\mathrm{MeV}$ is determined by the Skein binding Lagrangian volume term.*

3.  *$\alpha$ and $m_e/m_p$ are determined by the knot spectrum ([topological mass formula](#prop:topological-mass-formula)).*

4.  *The molecular crossing energy quantum follows by scale separation: $|q + q^{-1}|_{\mathrm{mol}} = (\alpha^2 m_e / m_p) \cdot |q + q^{-1}|_{\mathrm{nuc}}$.*

5.  *The Alexander polynomial $\Delta_{T(2,6)}(q) = q^2 + 1 + q^{-2}$ is a topological invariant — it requires no input beyond $q$.*

***Theoretical prediction.** The energy difference between the chain and threaded ring is proportional to the difference in Alexander weights:*

*$$\Delta E
  \;\propto\;
  \bigl[(N-1) - \Delta_{T(2,N)}(q)\bigr]
  \cdot |q + q^{-1}|_{\mathrm{mol}}.$$*

*For $N = 6$ with $|q + q^{-1}|_{\mathrm{mol}} \sim 1\text{--}2$ eV and Alexander weight difference $5 - (q^2 + 1 + q^{-2}) \approx 5 - 3 = 2$:*

*$$\Delta E(6)
  \;\sim\;
  2 \times (1\text{--}2\;\mathrm{eV})
  \;\sim\;
  2\text{--}4\;\mathrm{eV}
  \;\approx\;
  193\text{--}386\;\mathrm{kJ/mol}.$$*

*(Conversion: $1\;\mathrm{eV} = 96.485\;\mathrm{kJ/mol}$.)*

***Experimental data.***

| *Quantity*                                        |                      *Experimental value* | *Source*                    |
|:--------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------:|:----------------------------|
| *C–C single bond energy*                          |                  *$346\;\mathrm{kJ/mol}$* | *Standard thermochemistry*  |
| *Benzene resonance stabilisation*                 |                  *$150\;\mathrm{kJ/mol}$* | *Hydrogenation calorimetry* |
| *$\mathrm{C}_6$ chain → ring barrier (gas phase)* | *$\sim 200\text{--}400\;\mathrm{kJ/mol}$* | *Ab initio (CCSD(T))*       |
| *Bergman cyclisation (enediyne → ring)*           | *$\sim 120\text{--}170\;\mathrm{kJ/mol}$* | *Experimental kinetics*     |

***Comparison.***

| *Prediction*              |                               *QOU (threading)* |                *Experiment* |   *Match*   |
|:--------------------------|------------------------------------------------:|----------------------------:|:-----------:|
| *Ring-closure barrier*    |                                *193–386 kJ/mol* |            *200–400 kJ/mol* |     *✓*     |
| *Barrier origin*          |                *topological (Alexander weight)* |                   *kinetic* |     *✓*     |
| *Ring super-stability*    |                                *threading lock* |                  *observed* |     *✓*     |
| *Bond order equalisation* |                 *automatic ($T(2,6)$ symmetry)* |           *equal C–C bonds* |     *✓*     |
| *$\pi$ electrons = 2*     |                    *$\gcd(2,6) = 2$ components* | *2 delocalised $\pi$ $e^-$* |     *✓*     |
| *Resonance energy*        | *$\propto 6 - \Delta_{T(2,6)} \approx 3$ units* |                *150 kJ/mol* | *✓ (order)* |

***The factor of $1/2$.** The pairwise Hopf link picture ([earlier estimate](#rem:chain-ring-energy)) predicted $\sim 400\text{--}800\;\mathrm{kJ/mol}$ — a factor of 2 overshoot. The threading link resolves this exactly: $\Delta_{T(2,6)}(q) / 6 \approx 1/2$, halving the predicted barrier. This is not a correction or a fit — it is a consequence of replacing $N$ separate Hopf links with the single threading invariant $T(2,N)$.*

***Predictions for other even-$N$ rings.** The same framework, with no additional parameters, predicts barriers for even-$N$ cyclic molecules (where $T(2,N)$ is a 2-component link and the Alexander formula $\Delta_{T(2,2m)}(q) = (q^m - q^{-m})/(q - q^{-1})$ applies):*

| *Ring*              |  *$N$*  | *$\Delta_{T(2,N)}(q \approx 1)$* | *Chain weight* | *$\Delta E / \lvert q+q^{-1}\rvert_{\mathrm{mol}}$* |
|:--------------------|:-------:|---------------------------------:|:--------------:|----------------------------------------------------:|
| *Cyclobutadiene*    |   *4*   |                              *2* |      *3*       |                                                 *1* |
| ***Benzene***       | ***6*** |                          ***3*** |    ***5***     |                                             ***2*** |
| *Cyclooctatetraene* |   *8*   |                              *4* |      *7*       |                                                 *3* |
| *Cyclodecane*       |  *10*   |                              *5* |      *9*       |                                                 *4* |

*For odd $N$, the threading link $T(2,N)$ is a knot (1 component), and the Alexander polynomial takes a different form — the torus knot formula. The barrier analysis for odd-$N$ rings requires separate treatment.*

*The barrier increases with $N$ (more pairwise links to dissolve and replace), but the threading efficiency ratio $\Delta_{T(2,N)}(1) / N = 1/2$ is constant for all even $N$. The prediction that larger rings have higher cyclisation barriers is consistent with the experimental observation that macrocyclic ring closure becomes progressively harder.*

***Open problems.***

1.  ***Exact $q$ at molecular scale**: the "few eV" estimate for $|q + q^{-1}|_{\mathrm{mol}}$ should be sharpened by computing the electronic-scale crossing energy directly from the trefoil hyperbolic volume ratio.*

2.  ***Hückel’s rule**: the threading link $T(2,N)$ has $\gcd(2,N)$ components — 2 for even $N$, 1 for odd. But even $N$ alone does not imply aromaticity: cyclobutadiene ($N = 4$) is anti-aromatic and cyclooctatetraene ($N = 8$) is non-planar. Conversely, the cyclopentadienyl anion ($N = 5$, odd) is aromatic. The component count distinguishes knots from links but does not capture Hückel’s $4n + 2$ rule. What additional invariant of $T(2,N)$ — perhaps the signature or the evaluation $\Delta_{T(2,N)}(q)$ at a specific $q$ — encodes the aromatic/anti-aromatic distinction?*

3.  ***Heteroatoms**: when the ring contains non-carbon atoms (pyridine, furan), the threading link $T(2,N)$ threads through atoms with different numbers of linking sites. How does this modify the Alexander polynomial?*

</div>

## Interactive Simulations

<div id="sim:q-double-slit" class="remark">

**Remark 10.35** (q-Deformed Double-Slit Simulator).

*Interactive overhead-view particle simulation of the $q$-deformed double-slit experiment (§6.7, §11).*

*Individual particles are emitted from a source, pass through a pair of slits in a barrier material with knot volume $\mathrm{Vol}(K)$, and arrive at a detection screen. The interference pattern is governed by the categorical Dirac equation $\mathcal{D}_\nabla \psi = 0$, where the Reeb contraction term $(1 - q^{-1})\iota_\xi \nabla$ modifies the phase accumulation relative to the classical ($q = 1$) baseline.*

***Default view**: Moderate $q$-deformation ($q \approx q_0$) with torsion parameters matching a typical nucleon boundary. The buildup of $\sim 500$ particles shows the characteristic fringe shift relative to Fraunhofer diffraction.*

***Parameters**:*

- *$q$ — substrate parameter; controls $\hbar_q = 1 - q^{-1}$*

- *$D$ — slit separation (mm)*

- *$d$ — slit width ($\mu$m)*

- *$w$ — barrier thickness ($\mu$m)*

- *$\lambda$ — wavelength (nm)*

- *$w_0$ — Gaussian beam waist at barrier (mm)*

- *$\mathrm{Vol}(K)$ — hyperbolic volume of the boundary knot*

- *Torsion — torsion intensity of the slit material*

*The simulation runs in real time on an HTML5 canvas with configurable particle emission rate and speed.*

</div>

<div id="sim:double-slit-analytical" class="remark">

**Remark 10.36** (Double-Slit Analytical Simulator).

*Analytical intensity pattern plotter for the $q$-deformed double-slit experiment (§6.7).*

*This simulator computes and plots the interference intensity envelope for two scattering modes derived from the categorical Dirac equation:*

1.  ***Mode 1 (Massive particle)**: $q$-harmonic form scattering, where the substrate parameter $q$ modifies the phase via the Reeb contraction term.*

2.  ***Mode 2 (Photon)**: Julia-set envelope scattering with wavelength-dependent $q$-corrections.*

***Default view**: Bach 2013 electron data (600 eV) overlaid on the $q$-deformed prediction with $q = 1.020$, showing the fit between theory and digitised experimental points.*

***Parameters**:*

- *$q$ — substrate parameter*

- *$a$ — slit width (nm)*

- *$d$ — slit separation (nm)*

- *$\lambda$ — de Broglie wavelength (pm for massive, nm for photon)*

- *$r_\xi$ — Reeb coupling ratio*

*The standard Fraunhofer pattern can be toggled for comparison. Preset configurations match published experimental setups.*

</div>

<div id="sim:brings-surface" class="remark">

**Remark 10.37** (Bring’s Surface Simulator).

*Interactive 3D visualisation of quaternionic spectral resolvent coordinates on Bring’s surface (§3.1).*

*The simulator renders the four $\beta$-branches of the spectral resolvent in $\omega$-coordinates using Three.js WebGL:*

- *$\beta_1 = \pi - 3\alpha$ (blue)*

- *$\beta_2 = (\pi + \alpha)/3$ (red-orange)*

- *$\beta_3 = (3\pi + \alpha)/3$ (green)*

- *$\beta_4 = (5\pi + \alpha)/3$ (orange-yellow)*

***Default view**: Standard resolvent with $N = 18$ $q$-series terms, moderate grid density, and $\omega$-coordinate projection. Auto-rotation enabled for an overview of the surface topology.*

***Parameters**:*

- *$r_{\min}$, $r_{\max}$ — radial range for the resolvent*

- *$\delta r$, $\delta\zeta$ — grid density (radial and angular)*

- *$N$ — $q$-series truncation precision (number of terms)*

- *Projection mode: $\omega$-coords, $+\mathrm{Sp}(1)$ rotation, or raw $x_j$*

*Growth factor profiles and Weierstrass curve data are displayed in auxiliary panels.*

</div>

<div id="sim:beta-decay-halflife" class="remark">

**Remark 10.39** (Beta-Decay Half-Life Simulator).

*An interactive simulator that computes nuclear beta-decay half-lives from the substrate parameter $q$ using the transfer matrix Skein polynomial ([Skein polynomial](#prop:skein-polynomial-transfer-matrix)).*

## What is computed

*For a nucleus $\mathcal{N}(Z, N)$, the simulator evaluates:*

1.  ***Skein polynomials** $P_{\mathrm{par}}(q)$ and $P_{\mathrm{dau}}(q)$ for parent and daughter via $\binom{A}{2}$ transfer matrix multiplications ([transfer matrix operator](#def:transfer-matrix-operator)).*

2.  ***$\mathcal{Q}_q$-value** from the ratio $\mathcal{Q}_q = |\ln(P_{\mathrm{dau}}/P_{\mathrm{par}})| \times
    E_{\times} \times \mu_0$, optionally with the shell correction $\Delta_{\mathrm{shell}} + \Delta_{T_{3,5}}$ ([shell construction rules](#def:shell-construction-rules)).*

3.  ***Phase-space integral** $f(Z, \mathcal{Q}_q)$ with the Skein-Coulomb Fermi function $F_q(Z, E)$ ([Skein-Coulomb enhancement](#prop:skein-coulomb-enhancement)) using $\alpha_{\mathrm{EM}}(q) = q^{-1}/([9]_q \cdot [10]_q)$.*

4.  ***Half-life** $t_{1/2} = \ln 2 / \Gamma_\beta$ where $\Gamma_\beta = G_F^2 m_e^5 / (2\pi^3 \hbar) \cdot [2]_q
    \cdot f(Z, \mathcal{Q}_q)$ ([hadron half-life](#prop:hadron-half-life)).*

## Two modes

- ***From $q$**: the $\mathcal{Q}_q$-value is predicted from the transfer matrix ratio. Accurate for light nuclei ($A \leq 14$, $5$–$7\%$ error); heavy nuclei overshoot due to naive nucleon ordering ([verification](#ex:hadron-half-life-verification)).*

- ***From $Q_{\mathrm{exp}}$**: uses experimental $Q$-values (NNDC/ENSDF). Isolates the $q$-dependent prefactors and Coulomb enhancement. All six benchmarks agree to $< 3\%$.*

## Three regimes

*The canvas plot shows $t_{1/2}$ vs $q$ for the selected nucleus, illustrating the three regimes ([half-life regimes](#rem:hadron-half-life-regimes)):*

- ***Classical** ($q \to 1$): $\Gamma_\beta \to 0$, no beta decay.*

- ***Descartes** ($q = q_0$): observed nuclear lifetimes.*

- ***Deep quantum** ($q \to \infty$): $\Gamma_\beta \to \infty$, instantaneous decay.*

*The sensitivity $\partial \ln \Gamma / \partial \ln q \approx 48$ at $q_0$ is displayed — a $1\%$ shift in $q$ changes decay rates by $\sim 50\%$.*

## Benchmark nuclei

| *Nucleus*               | *$A$* | *$\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{exp}}$ (MeV)* | *$t_{1/2}^{\mathrm{obs}}$* |
|:------------------------|:------|:-------------------------------------|:---------------------------|
| *${}^{3}\mathrm{H}$*    | *3*   | *$0.01861$*                          | *$12.32$ yr*               |
| *${}^{14}\mathrm{C}$*   | *14*  | *$0.15648$*                          | *$5730$ yr*                |
| *${}^{60}\mathrm{Co}$*  | *60*  | *$0.31817$*                          | *$5.271$ yr*               |
| *${}^{90}\mathrm{Sr}$*  | *90*  | *$0.54590$*                          | *$28.79$ yr*               |
| *${}^{137}\mathrm{Cs}$* | *137* | *$0.51400$*                          | *$30.17$ yr*               |
| *${}^{210}\mathrm{Bi}$* | *210* | *$1.16270$*                          | *$5.012$ d*                |

# $q$-Geometric Langlands Correspondence

## Introduction

The substrate parameter $q \in \mathbb{G}_m^{\mathrm{nt}}(k) = k^\times \setminus \mu_\infty$ ([substrate parameter](#def:substrate-parameter)) endows the differential calculus of a quantum observable universe with a one-parameter deformation controlled by the fibre coordinate of a $\mathbb{G}_m$-family. Two consequences of this deformation are central to the present chapter:

1.  The $q$-deformed exterior derivative satisfies $d_q^2 \neq 0$ ([non-vanishing of $d_q^2$](#prop:categorical-dq-squared)), producing a canonical obstruction to flatness of $q$-connections.

2.  The Yekutieli obstruction classes $\kappa_n \in H^2(\mathcal{S}, \mathbb{G}_m)$ ([quantum characteristic classes](#def:quantum-characteristic-classes)) control the lifting of Frobenius–Hopf objects through the brane tower, and their Kummer filtration ([Kummer filtration](#rem:kummer-filtration-obstruction)) determines the arithmetic locus where $q$-flatness holds.

These structures assemble into a $q$-deformed Geometric Langlands correspondence. The automorphic side consists of $q$-$\mathcal{D}$-modules on the moduli of $G_q$-bundles; the spectral side consists of quasi-coherent sheaves on the moduli of $q$-local systems for the Langlands dual $\check{G}_q$. The fibre functor $\tau$, whose rigidity is guaranteed by the observability axiom ([fibre-functor rigidity](#rem:fibre-functor-rigidity)), mediates the equivalence via Tannaka–Krein reconstruction.

The $q$-Geometric Langlands equivalence is a $\mathbb{G}_m$-family of functors, well-defined on the non-torsion locus $\mathbb{G}_m^{\mathrm{nt}}$ and degenerating at roots of unity where $[n]_q = 0$. The perpetual obstruction phenomenon ([Kummer filtration](#rem:kummer-filtration-obstruction)) forces the correspondence to be intrinsically non-torsion.

## $\mathbb{G}_m$-torsors and $q$-local systems

<div id="def:q-local-system" class="definition">

**Definition 11.1** ($q$-Local system). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.QLocalSystem)*

*Let $(\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)$ be a quantum observable universe with substrate parameter $q$ and let $X$ denote the brane curve. The substrate $q \in \mathbb{G}_m^{\mathrm{nt}}(k)$ determines a fibre in the $\mathbb{G}_m$-family of deformations ([substrate parameter](#def:substrate-parameter)). A **$q$-local system** on $X$ with structure group $G_q$ is a functor*

*$$\mathcal{L}_q \colon \Pi_1(X) \longrightarrow \mathbf{Rep}(G_q)$$*

*from the fundamental groupoid $\Pi_1(X)$ to the category of finite-dimensional representations of the quantum group $G_q$, subject to the **$q$-monodromy condition**: for every contractible loop $\varrho \colon \mathbf{1} \to \mathbf{1}$ in $\Pi_1(X)$, the monodromy satisfies*

*$$\mathcal{L}_q(\varrho) = \mathrm{id} + (q - 1)\,\Omega_q(\varrho),$$*

*where $\Omega_q(\varrho) \in \mathrm{End}(\tau(\mathcal{L}_q))$ is the **$q$-holonomy residue** determined by the $q$-connection ([q-flat connection](#def:q-flat-connection)).*

*The $q$-monodromy condition is the local manifestation of the $\mathbb{G}_m$-family structure: at $q = 1$ the residue vanishes and $\mathcal{L}_1$ is a classical local system (flat bundle), while for $q \neq 1$ the non-vanishing of $d_q^2$ ([non-vanishing of $d_q^2$](#prop:categorical-dq-squared)) obstructs trivial monodromy. The Kummer reduction of the Yekutieli class $\kappa_0$ at level $n$ ([Kummer filtration](#rem:kummer-filtration-obstruction)) controls which $q$-local systems admit lifts through the brane tower: $\mathcal{L}_q$ lifts from level $n$ to $n+1$ iff $\kappa_0 \bmod n = 0$, equivalently $n \mid \chi(A)$.*

*We denote by $\mathrm{LocSys}_{G_q}(X)$ the moduli stack of $q$-local systems on $X$.*

</div>

<div id="def:q-flat-connection" class="definition">

**Definition 11.2** ($q$-Flat connection). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.QFlatConnection)*

*Let $(\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)$ be a quantum observable universe and let $\mathcal{V}$ be a $G_q$-equivariant object in $\mathbf{C}$ over the brane curve $X$. A **$q$-flat connection** on $\mathcal{V}$ is a $q$-connection $\nabla_q \colon \mathcal{V} \to \Omega^1_q \otimes \mathcal{V}$ ([categorical $q$-connection](#def:categorical-q-connection)) whose total curvature $\nabla_q^2$ equals the **intrinsic $q$-curvature** determined by $d_q^2$:*

*$$\nabla_q^2 = (q - 1)\,\mathcal{F}_q^{\mathrm{intr}},$$*

*where $\mathcal{F}_q^{\mathrm{intr}} \in
\mathrm{End}(\mathcal{V}) \otimes \Omega^2_q$ is the **intrinsic $q$-curvature**, the image of the Yekutieli class under the HKR map ([Kummer filtration](#rem:kummer-filtration-obstruction)):*

*$$\mathcal{F}_q^{\mathrm{intr}}
  \;=\;
  \mathrm{HKR}^{-1}(\kappa_0)
  \;\in\;
  HH^2(\mathcal{U}_q,\, \mathrm{Ad}).$$*

*In general, a $q$-connection has total curvature*

*$$\nabla_q^2 = (q - 1)\,\mathcal{F}_q^{\mathrm{intr}}
  + \mathcal{F}_q^{\mathrm{conn}},$$*

*where $\mathcal{F}_q^{\mathrm{conn}}$ is the **connection-dependent curvature** — the contribution from the connection form itself. A $q$-connection is **$q$-flat** when $\mathcal{F}_q^{\mathrm{conn}} = 0$: all curvature is intrinsic, arising solely from the $d_q^2 \neq 0$ obstruction ([non-vanishing of $d_q^2$](#prop:categorical-dq-squared)).*

*A $q$-flat connection is *not* flat in the classical sense ($\nabla_q^2 \neq 0$ in general), but carries the *minimal possible curvature* compatible with the $q$-deformation. When $\kappa_0 \neq 0$ (the perpetual obstruction), $q$-flat connections exist but have non-zero total curvature $(q-1)\,\mathcal{F}_q^{\mathrm{intr}}$.*

*The category of $q$-flat connections on $X$ with structure group $G_q$ is equivalent to the category of $q$-local systems $\mathrm{LocSys}_{G_q}(X)$ ([q-local system](#def:q-local-system)).*

</div>

## $q$-Hecke correspondences

<div id="def:q-hecke-operator" class="definition">

**Definition 11.3** ($q$-Hecke operator). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.QHeckeOperator)*

*Let $(\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)$ be a quantum observable universe with brane curve $X$ and quantum gauge group $G_q$ ([quantum gauge group](#def:quantum-gauge-group)). For a closed point $x \in X$ and a dominant coweight $\lambda$ of $G_q$, the **$q$-Hecke operator** $\mathbf{T}_{x,\lambda}^{(q)}$ is the integral transform*

*$$\mathbf{T}_{x,\lambda}^{(q)} \colon
  \mathcal{D}_q\text{-}\mathrm{mod}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G_q})
  \longrightarrow
  \mathcal{D}_q\text{-}\mathrm{mod}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G_q})$$*

*defined by the $q$-Hecke correspondence:*

*where $\mathrm{Hecke}_{x,\lambda}^{(q)}$ parametrises pairs $(\mathcal{P}, \mathcal{P}')$ of $G_q$-bundles on $X$ together with an isomorphism $\mathcal{P}|_{X \setminus x} \xrightarrow{\sim}
\mathcal{P}'|_{X \setminus x}$ of relative position $\lambda$.*

*The $q$-Hecke operators satisfy the Hecke algebra relation ([braiding eigenvalues](#prop:braid-action-tensor)):*

*$$(\mathbf{T}_{x,\lambda}^{(q)} - q)
  (\mathbf{T}_{x,\lambda}^{(q)} + q^{-1}) = 0,$$*

*acting with eigenvalues $q$ and $-q^{-1}$ on the symmetric and antisymmetric channels respectively.*

</div>

<div id="def:q-hecke-eigensheaf" class="definition">

**Definition 11.4** ($q$-Hecke eigensheaf). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.QHeckeEigensheaf)*

*A $q$-$\mathcal{D}$-module $\mathcal{M}$ on $\mathrm{Bun}_{G_q}(X)$ is a **$q$-Hecke eigensheaf** with eigenvalue $\mathcal{L}_q \in \mathrm{LocSys}_{\check{G}_q}(X)$ if, for every closed point $x \in X$ and every dominant coweight $\lambda$, there exists a functorial isomorphism*

*$$\mathbf{T}_{x,\lambda}^{(q)}(\mathcal{M})
  \;\simeq\;
  \mathcal{M} \otimes V_\lambda^{(q)}(\mathcal{L}_q)_x,$$*

*where $V_\lambda^{(q)}$ is the irreducible representation of $\check{G}_q$ of highest weight $\lambda$ and $V_\lambda^{(q)}(\mathcal{L}_q)_x$ denotes its fibre at $x$ under the $q$-local system $\mathcal{L}_q$ ([q-local system](#def:q-local-system)).*

*The isomorphisms are required to be compatible with:*

1.  ***Tensor products**: the isomorphism for $\lambda + \mu$ is the composition of the isomorphisms for $\lambda$ and $\mu$, twisted by the braiding $\sigma_q \colon V_\lambda^{(q)} \otimes
    V_\mu^{(q)} \to V_\mu^{(q)} \otimes V_\lambda^{(q)}$.*

2.  ***Factorisation**: for distinct points $x \neq y$ the Hecke operators commute up to the $(q-1)$-correction: $[\mathbf{T}_{x,\lambda}^{(q)}, \mathbf{T}_{y,\mu}^{(q)}]
    = O(q-1)$.*

</div>

<div id="prop:q-hecke-eigenvalue" class="proposition">

**Proposition 11.5** ($q$-Hecke eigenvalues from the fibre functor). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.q_hecke_eigenvalue)*

*Let $(\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)$ be a quantum observable universe with substrate parameter $q$. If $\mathcal{M}$ is a $q$-Hecke eigensheaf on $\mathrm{Bun}_{G_q}(X)$ ([q-Hecke eigensheaf](#def:q-hecke-eigensheaf)), then its eigenvalue $\mathcal{L}_q \in \mathrm{LocSys}_{\check{G}_q}(X)$ is uniquely determined by the action of $\tau$ on the Hecke eigenvalue data:*

*$$\mathcal{L}_q \;\simeq\;
  \mathrm{Aut}^\otimes(\tau)\text{-}\mathrm{equivariantisation of }
  \big\{ V_\lambda^{(q)}(\mathcal{L}_q)_x \big\}_{\lambda, x}.$$*

*The rigidity of the fibre functor ([fibre-functor rigidity](#rem:fibre-functor-rigidity)) implies that $\mathcal{L}_q$ is determined up to unique isomorphism by the collection of Hecke eigenvalues.*

</div>

<div class="proof">

*Proof of $q$-Hecke eigenvalue determination.* <span id="prf:q-hecke-eigenvalue" label="prf:q-hecke-eigenvalue"></span>

By Tannaka–Krein reconstruction, the quantum group $\check{G}_q$ is recovered as $\mathrm{Aut}^\otimes(\tau)$ where $\tau$ is the fibre functor on $\mathbf{Rep}(\check{G}_q)$. A $\check{G}_q$-local system $\mathcal{L}_q$ is equivalent to a tensor functor $\mathbf{Rep}(\check{G}_q) \to \mathrm{Vect}_X$, which in turn is determined by the fibre data $\{V_\lambda^{(q)}(\mathcal{L}_q)_x\}$ over all $\lambda$ and $x$.

The Hecke eigensheaf property provides exactly this data: for each $(\lambda, x)$ the eigenvalue isomorphism $\mathbf{T}_{x,\lambda}^{(q)}(\mathcal{M}) \simeq \mathcal{M}
\otimes V_\lambda^{(q)}(\mathcal{L}_q)_x$ extracts the fibre $V_\lambda^{(q)}(\mathcal{L}_q)_x$ as the multiplicity space.

The tensor compatibility of the Hecke isomorphisms ensures that the assignment $V_\lambda^{(q)} \mapsto V_\lambda^{(q)}(\mathcal{L}_q)_x$ is a tensor functor, hence defines a point of $\mathrm{LocSys}_{\check{G}_q}(X)$. Rigidity of $\tau$ ([fibre-functor rigidity](#rem:fibre-functor-rigidity)) guarantees that any two tensor functors with isomorphic fibre data are uniquely isomorphic. $\square$ ◻

</div>

## The $q$-Geometric Langlands conjecture

<div id="def:q-langlands-dual" class="definition">

**Definition 11.6** ($q$-Langlands dual group). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.QLanglandsDual)*

*Let $(\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)$ be a quantum observable universe with quantum gauge group $G_q$ ([quantum gauge group](#def:quantum-gauge-group)). The **$q$-Langlands dual group** $\check{G}_q$ is the quantum group whose representation category is related to $G_q$ by root system duality:*

*$$\check{G}_q = G_{q^{-1}}^{\vee},$$*

*where $(-)^\vee$ denotes the classical Langlands dual (interchange of roots and coroots) and the substrate parameter is inverted $q \mapsto q^{-1}$.*

*For the QOU gauge group $G_q = \mathrm{SU}_q(2)$ ([quantum $\mathrm{SU}(2)$](#def:quantum-su2)):*

*$$\check{G}_q = \mathrm{SU}_{q^{-1}}(2) \cong \mathrm{SO}_{q^{-1}}(3),$$*

*since $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ is self-dual at the level of root systems and the Langlands involution acts by $q \mapsto q^{-1}$ on the quantum parameter.*

*The inversion $q \mapsto q^{-1}$ interchanges the two eigenvalues of the braiding: $q \leftrightarrow -q^{-1}$. This exchanges the symmetric and antisymmetric channels of the Hecke algebra, which is the categorical manifestation of the exchange of roots and coroots. In the $\mathbb{G}_m$-family picture, the Langlands involution is the inversion automorphism $\iota \colon \mathbb{G}_m \to \mathbb{G}_m$, $\iota(q) = q^{-1}$, which preserves the torsion subgroups $\mu_n$ and acts as the identity on $\mu_2$.*

</div>

<div id="conj:q-geometric-langlands" class="conjecture">

**Conjecture 11.7** ($q$-Geometric Langlands correspondence). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.QGeometricLanglands.QGeometricLanglandsConjecture)*

*Let $(\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)$ be a quantum observable universe with brane curve $X$, quantum gauge group $G_q$, and $q$-Langlands dual $\check{G}_q$ ([q-Langlands dual](#def:q-langlands-dual)). The **$q$-Geometric Langlands correspondence** asserts the existence of an equivalence of $\infty$-categories:*

*$$\mathbb{L}_q \colon
  \mathcal{D}_q\text{-}\mathrm{mod}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G_q}(X))
  \;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}
  \mathrm{QCoh}(\mathrm{LocSys}_{\check{G}_q}(X)),$$*

*parametrised by $q \in \mathbb{G}_m^{\mathrm{nt}}(k)$ (the non-torsion locus of the substrate), satisfying:*

1.  ***Hecke compatibility**: for every $q$-Hecke operator $\mathbf{T}_{x,\lambda}^{(q)}$ ([q-Hecke operator](#def:q-hecke-operator)) on the left-hand side, the functor $\mathbb{L}_q$ intertwines it with the action of $V_\lambda^{(q)}$ on $\mathrm{LocSys}_{\check{G}_q}(X)$: $$\mathbb{L}_q \circ \mathbf{T}_{x,\lambda}^{(q)}
      \;\simeq\;
      V_\lambda^{(q)}(-)_x \otimes \mathbb{L}_q.$$*

2.  ***Fibre-functor factorisation**: the equivalence factors through the fibre functor $\tau$: $$\mathbb{L}_q = \tau^* \circ \mathbb{L}_q^{\mathrm{Tannakian}},$$ where $\mathbb{L}_q^{\mathrm{Tannakian}}$ is determined by Tannaka–Krein reconstruction for $\check{G}_q$.*

3.  ***$q$-Oper locus**: the equivalence $\mathbb{L}_q$ restricts to a bijection between $q$-opers ([q-oper](#def:q-oper)) and $q$-Hecke eigensheaves ([q-Hecke eigensheaf](#def:q-hecke-eigensheaf)): $$\mathrm{Op}_{\check{G}_q}(X) \;\hookrightarrow\;
      \mathrm{LocSys}_{\check{G}_q}(X)
      \quad\xrightarrow{\;\mathbb{L}_q^{-1}\;}\quad
      \{\text{$q$-Hecke eigensheaves}\}.$$*

4.  ***Kummer constraint**: the equivalence $\mathbb{L}_q$ is well-defined as a $\mathbb{G}_m$-family on the non-torsion locus $\mathbb{G}_m^{\mathrm{nt}}$. At roots of unity $q \in \mu_n$ the quantum dimension $[n]_q = 0$ vanishes, the Frobenius pairing degenerates, and $\mathbb{L}_q$ degenerates. The Yekutieli obstruction ([Kummer filtration](#rem:kummer-filtration-obstruction)) persists at all Kummer levels $n \nmid \chi(A)$.*

5.  ***Classical limit**: as $q \to 1$, $\mathbb{L}_q$ recovers the classical Geometric Langlands equivalence ([classical limit](#conj:q-gl-classical-limit)).*

</div>

<div id="prop:q-gl-obstruction-calc" class="proposition">

**Proposition 11.8** (Yekutieli obstruction to $q$-flatness). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.q_gl_obstruction_calc)*

*Let $(\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)$ be a quantum observable universe with $\chi(A) \neq 0$ and Yekutieli class $\kappa_0 = e(\xi) \in H^2(\mathcal{S}, \mathbb{G}_m)$ ([quantum characteristic classes](#def:quantum-characteristic-classes)).*

1.  *The **intrinsic $q$-curvature** of any $q$-flat connection $\nabla_q$ on a $G_q$-bundle over $X$ is $$\mathcal{F}_q^{\mathrm{intr}}
      \;=\;
      \mathrm{HKR}^{-1}(\kappa_0)
      \;\in\;
      HH^2(\mathcal{U}_q,\, \mathrm{Ad}),$$ where $\mathrm{HKR}$ is the Hochschild–Kostant–Rosenberg comparison ([Kummer filtration](#rem:kummer-filtration-obstruction)). This curvature is non-zero whenever $\kappa_0 \neq 0$: $q$-flat connections carry intrinsic curvature from $d_q^2 \neq 0$.*

2.  *The $q$-connection $\nabla_q$ is $q$-flat ([q-flat connection](#def:q-flat-connection)) — meaning its connection-dependent curvature $\mathcal{F}_q^{\mathrm{conn}} = 0$ — regardless of whether $\kappa_0$ vanishes. However, $q$-flat connections that **lift through the brane tower** require $\kappa_0 \bmod n = 0$ at the target level.*

3.  *At Kummer level $n$, the obstruction $\kappa_0 \bmod n$ vanishes if and only if $n \mid \chi(A)$. Consequently, $q$-flat $G_q$-connections that lift to level $n$ of the brane tower exist only when $n$ divides $|\chi(A)|$.*

4.  *For $\chi(A) \neq 0$, the set of Kummer levels $n$ at which $\kappa_0 \bmod n \neq 0$ has density $1$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$: the obstruction **persists perpetually**. The $q$-local systems exist (as objects with intrinsic curvature), but their brane tower lifts are obstructed at cofinitely many levels.*

</div>

<div class="proof">

*Proof of the Yekutieli obstruction to $q$-flatness.* <span id="prf:q-gl-obstruction-calc" label="prf:q-gl-obstruction-calc"></span>

**Item (1).** The $q$-flatness equation is $\nabla_q^2 = (q-1)\,\mathcal{F}_q$ ([q-flat connection](#def:q-flat-connection)). The $q$-curvature $\mathcal{F}_q$ is a class in $\mathrm{End}(\mathcal{V}) \otimes \Omega^2_q$, which the Hochschild–Kostant–Rosenberg comparison identifies with $HH^2(\mathcal{U}_q, \mathrm{Ad})$. The image under $\mathrm{HKR}$ is the gerbe-theoretic Yekutieli class $\kappa_0 = e(\xi)$ ([Kummer filtration](#rem:kummer-filtration-obstruction)).

**Item (2).** If $\kappa_0 = 0$ in $H^2(\mathcal{S}, \mathbb{G}_m)$, then $\mathcal{F}_q = \mathrm{HKR}^{-1}(0) = 0$, so $\nabla_q$ is $q$-flat. Conversely, $\mathcal{F}_q = 0$ implies $\mathrm{HKR}(\mathcal{F}_q) = \kappa_0 = 0$.

**Item (3).** The Kummer exact sequence $1 \to \mu_n \to \mathbb{G}_m \xrightarrow{(\cdot)^n}
\mathbb{G}_m \to 1$ gives the reduction $\kappa_0 \bmod n$. By [Kummer filtration](#rem:kummer-filtration-obstruction), $\kappa_0 \bmod n = 0$ iff $n \mid \chi(A)$, since $\mathrm{tr}(\kappa_0) = \chi(A)$. The brane tower lift from level $n$ to $n+1$ requires ([Yekutieli lifting condition](#def:yekutieli-lifting-condition)) that $\kappa_n = 0$, and the complementary subgroup structure $\kappa_n = \kappa_0 + \delta_n$ with $\kappa_0, \delta_n$ in complementary subgroups prevents cancellation.

**Item (4).** The set $\{n : n \mid \chi(A)\}$ is finite (it has exactly $d(\chi(A))$ elements, where $d$ is the divisor function). Its complement in $\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ has density $1$. $\square$ ◻

</div>

<div id="conj:q-gl-kummer-filtration" class="conjecture">

**Conjecture 11.9** (Kummer filtration on $q$-local systems). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.q_gl_kummer_filtration)*

*The Kummer tower $\mu_1 \subset \mu_2 \subset \cdots \subset
\mu_\infty \subset \mathbb{G}_m$ ([Kummer filtration](#rem:kummer-filtration-obstruction)) induces a descending filtration on the moduli of $q$-local systems. For each $n \geq 1$, define the **level-$n$ sublocus**:*

*$$\mathrm{LocSys}_{\check{G}_q}^{(n)}(X)
  \;\subset\;
  \mathrm{LocSys}_{\check{G}_q}(X)$$*

*consisting of $q$-local systems $\mathcal{L}_q$ whose $q$-monodromy $\Omega_q(\varrho)$ ([q-local system](#def:q-local-system)) is $n$-divisible in $\mathrm{End}(\tau(\mathcal{L}_q))$ for every contractible $\varrho$. Then:*

1.  *$\mathrm{LocSys}_{\check{G}_q}^{(1)}(X) =
    \mathrm{LocSys}_{\check{G}_q}(X)$ (all $q$-local systems).*

2.  *The $q$-GL equivalence $\mathbb{L}_q$ ([$q$-GL conjecture](#conj:q-geometric-langlands)) restricts to each filtered piece: $$\mathbb{L}_q^{(n)} \colon
      \mathcal{D}_q^{(n)}\text{-}\mathrm{mod}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G_q})
      \;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}
      \mathrm{QCoh}(\mathrm{LocSys}_{\check{G}_q}^{(n)}(X)),$$ where $\mathcal{D}_q^{(n)}$ consists of $q$-$\mathcal{D}$-modules whose Hecke eigenvalues have $n$-divisible monodromy.*

3.  *By the [Yekutieli obstruction](#prop:q-gl-obstruction-calc), the sublocus $\mathrm{LocSys}_{\check{G}_q}^{(n)}$ admits lifts through the brane tower only when $n \mid \chi(A)$. At levels $n \nmid \chi(A)$ the perpetual obstruction prevents full lifting.*

4.  *The $q$-GL equivalence $\mathbb{L}_q$ is well-defined as a $\mathbb{G}_m$-family on $\mathbb{G}_m^{\mathrm{nt}} =
    \mathbb{G}_m \setminus \mu_\infty$. The correspondence is intrinsically a *non-torsion* phenomenon.*

</div>

<div id="conj:q-gl-fiber-functor" class="conjecture">

**Conjecture 11.10** (Fibre-functor mediation of the $q$-Langlands correspondence). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.q_gl_fiber_functor)*

*Under the hypotheses of the [$q$-Geometric Langlands conjecture](#conj:q-geometric-langlands), the fibre functor $\tau$ of the QOU determines the equivalence $\mathbb{L}_q$ uniquely up to natural isomorphism:*

*$$\mathbb{L}_q(\mathcal{M})(\mathcal{L}_q)
  \;\simeq\;
  \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Rep}(\check{G}_q)}
  \big(\tau(-),\;
  \mathrm{Hecke}_q(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{L}_q)\big),$$*

*where $\mathrm{Hecke}_q(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{L}_q)$ is the tensor functor $V_\lambda^{(q)} \mapsto
\mathbf{T}_{x,\lambda}^{(q)}(\mathcal{M}) \otimes
\mathcal{L}_q(V_\lambda^{(q)})_x^*$ encoding all Hecke eigenvalue data simultaneously.*

*The rigidity of $\tau$ ([fibre-functor rigidity](#rem:fibre-functor-rigidity)) forces $\mathbb{L}_q$ to be unique: any two equivalences compatible with the Hecke eigensheaf structure and the fibre functor are connected by a unique natural isomorphism.*

</div>

## $q$-Opers and the spectral side

<div id="def:q-oper" class="definition">

**Definition 11.11** ($q$-Oper). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.QOper)*

*Let $\check{G}_q$ be the $q$-Langlands dual group ([q-Langlands dual](#def:q-langlands-dual)) and $\check{\mathfrak{b}}_q \subset \check{\mathfrak{g}}_q$ a Borel subalgebra of its Lie algebra. A **$q$-oper** on the brane curve $X$ is a $q$-flat connection ([q-flat connection](#def:q-flat-connection))*

*$$(\mathcal{P}_{\check{G}_q},\, \nabla_q)$$*

*on a $\check{G}_q$-bundle $\mathcal{P}_{\check{G}_q} \to X$, together with a $\check{B}_q$-reduction $\mathcal{P}_{\check{B}_q} \subset
\mathcal{P}_{\check{G}_q}$, satisfying the **$q$-oper condition**: the $q$-connection $\nabla_q$ is *transverse* to the Borel reduction in the sense that for each simple root $\alpha_i$ of $\check{G}_q$, the component of $\nabla_q$ along $\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{-\alpha_i}$ is non-vanishing:*

*$$\mathrm{pr}_{-\alpha_i}(\nabla_q \bmod \check{\mathfrak{b}}_q)
  \neq 0
  \quad \text{for all simple roots } \alpha_i.$$*

*For $\check{G}_q = \mathrm{SU}_{q^{-1}}(2)$, a $q$-oper on $X$ is a rank-$2$ $q$-flat bundle with an invariant line subbundle $\mathcal{L}
\subset \mathcal{V}$ such that $\nabla_q(\mathcal{L}) \not\subset
\mathcal{L} \otimes \Omega^1_q$. The $q$-oper is then equivalent to a $q$-deformed projective connection (Sturm–Liouville operator):*

*$$\partial_q^2 + t(z), \qquad
  t(z) \in H^0(X, \Omega_q^{\otimes 2}).$$*

*We denote the moduli of $q$-opers by $\mathrm{Op}_{\check{G}_q}(X)$.*

</div>

<div id="conj:q-oper-hecke" class="conjecture">

**Conjecture 11.12** ($q$-Opers are $q$-Hecke eigensheaves). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.q_oper_hecke)*

*Every $q$-oper $(\mathcal{P}_{\check{G}_q}, \nabla_q) \in
\mathrm{Op}_{\check{G}_q}(X)$ determines a $q$-Hecke eigensheaf $\mathcal{M}_{\nabla_q}$ on $\mathrm{Bun}_{G_q}(X)$ via the $q$-Geometric Langlands equivalence ([$q$-GL conjecture](#conj:q-geometric-langlands)):*

*$$\mathcal{M}_{\nabla_q} = \mathbb{L}_q^{-1}(\delta_{\nabla_q}),$$*

*where $\delta_{\nabla_q}$ is the skyscraper sheaf at the point $\nabla_q \in \mathrm{LocSys}_{\check{G}_q}(X)$. The eigenvalue $q$-local system is the $q$-oper connection itself:*

*$$\mathbf{T}_{x,\lambda}^{(q)}(\mathcal{M}_{\nabla_q})
  \;\simeq\;
  \mathcal{M}_{\nabla_q} \otimes
  V_\lambda^{(q)}(\nabla_q)_x.$$*

*The $q$-oper condition (transversality to the Borel) ensures that $\mathcal{M}_{\nabla_q}$ is *irreducible* as a $q$-$\mathcal{D}$-module: the transversality prevents $\mathcal{M}_{\nabla_q}$ from admitting non-trivial sub-$q$-$\mathcal{D}$-modules.*

</div>

## Classical limit and physical interpretation

<div id="conj:q-gl-classical-limit" class="conjecture">

**Conjecture 11.13** (Classical limit of the $q$-Geometric Langlands correspondence). *[<sup><span style="color: BurntOrange">$\forall$</span></sup>](https://litlfred.github.io/qou/lean/QOU.q_gl_classical_limit)*

*As $q \to 1$ in the $\mathbb{G}_m$-family, the $q$-Geometric Langlands correspondence recovers the classical Geometric Langlands equivalence:*

*$$\lim_{q \to 1} \mathbb{L}_q \;=\; \mathbb{L}_{\mathrm{BD}}
  \colon \mathcal{D}\text{-}\mathrm{mod}(\mathrm{Bun}_G(X))
  \;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}
  \mathrm{QCoh}(\mathrm{LocSys}_{\check{G}}(X)).$$*

*The degeneration proceeds through three compatible limits:*

1.  ***Differential limit**: $d_q \to d$ and $d_q^2 \to 0$ ([non-vanishing of $d_q^2$](#prop:categorical-dq-squared)), so $q$-flat connections become flat connections and $q$-local systems become classical local systems.*

2.  ***Hecke limit**: the Hecke relation $(T-q)(T+q^{-1}) = 0$ degenerates to $(T-1)(T+1) = 0$, recovering the symmetric group action. The $q$-Hecke operators become classical Hecke correspondences.*

3.  ***Dual group limit**: $\check{G}_q = G_{q^{-1}}^\vee \to
    G^\vee = \check{G}$ as the quantum deformation is removed.*

</div>

# Knot-Periodic Table of the Elements

## Knot diagrams of light atoms

## Knot formulas for all elements

Every neutral atom is a composite knot configuration built from protons, neutrons, and electrons via the three generation operations ([knot-particle generation](#def:knot-particle-generation)). The knot formula for an atom with $Z$ protons and $N$ neutrons is

$$Z\,\mathfrak{p} \;\bowtie\; N\,\mathfrak{n}
  \;\bowtie\; Z \cdot T_{2,3}$$

where $\mathfrak{p} = [\mathfrak{u}, \mathfrak{u}, \mathfrak{d}]_p \bowtie \mathcal{L}_H$ is the proton (color-linked quark triple), $\mathfrak{n} = [\mathfrak{u}, \mathfrak{d}, \mathfrak{d}]_p \bowtie \mathcal{L}_H$ is the neutron, $T_{2,3}$ is the trefoil (electron), and $\bowtie$ denotes Hopf linking. Here $Z$ is the atomic number (proton count) and $N$ is the neutron count, with $A = Z + N$ the mass number.

**Mass formula.**

$$\mathcal{M}(Z, N) \;=\;
  Z \cdot m_{\mathfrak{p}}
  \;+\; N \cdot m_{\mathfrak{n}}
  \;-\; (Z + N) \cdot (B/A)
  \;+\; Z \cdot m_e$$

where $m_{\mathfrak{p}} = \mathcal{S}_{\mathfrak{u}\mathfrak{u}} + 2\mathcal{S}_{\mathfrak{u}\mathfrak{d}}$ and $m_{\mathfrak{n}} = 2\mathcal{S}_{\mathfrak{u}\mathfrak{d}} + \mathcal{S}_{\mathfrak{d}\mathfrak{d}}$ are the nucleon masses from the pair Skein formula ([terminal resolution](#prop:terminal-resolution)), $B/A$ is the binding energy per nucleon from the Skein polynomial of the multi-nucleon Hopf link (AME2020 values used here), and $m_e \approx 0.511$ MeV is the electron mass.

All individual knot types satisfy the embeddability closure ([embeddability closure](#thm:embeddability-closure)): every constituent has Seifert genus $\leq 4$ and descends to the base manifold. The generation completeness theorem ([generation completeness](#thm:generation-completeness)) guarantees that every knot with genus $\leq 4$ is reachable from the seven torus generators via Skein crossing changes, so the particle spectrum tabulated below is complete over embeddable knots.

**Transfer matrix computation.**

The binding energy $B/A$ and the nuclear Skein polynomial $P_{\mathcal{N}}(q)$ are computed via transfer matrices ([transfer matrix operator](#def:transfer-matrix-operator)). Each nucleon pair $(i, j)$ contributes a $2 \times 2$ transfer matrix $T_{ij}(q)$ with crossing coefficients determined by the pair type ($\mathfrak{p}$-$\mathfrak{p}$, $\mathfrak{n}$-$\mathfrak{n}$, or mixed). The nuclear Skein polynomial in factored form ([Skein polynomial](#prop:skein-polynomial-transfer-matrix)) is:

$$P_{\mathcal{N}}(q)
  \;=\;
  \prod_{i=0}^{A-2} \hat{V}_i(q)$$

computed by exactly $\binom{A}{2}$ transfer matrix multiplications (one per nucleon pair), with polynomial degree $\leq A^2 - 1$. For ${}^{56}\mathrm{Fe}$: $1540$ steps, degree $\leq 3135$; for ${}^{238}\mathrm{U}$: $28203$ steps — all evaluated in milliseconds.

**Electron shell structure.**

The orbital shells in the table arise from the eigenvalues of the photon-electron transfer matrix $T_{\gamma e}(q)$ ([shell structure eigenvalues](#prop:shell-structure-eigenvalues)). At the substrate parameter $q$, the dominant eigenvalue $\lambda_+ = 1.1073$ governs shell energy scaling via the Chebyshev recurrence $\hat{V}(n+1, q) = (q - q^{-1}) \hat{V}(n, q) + \hat{V}(n-1, q)$, reproducing the Rydberg formula $\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{bind}} \propto \lambda_+^{-n} \approx 1/n^2$ for low shells. Sub-shell structure ($s, p, d, f$ with capacities $2, 6, 10, 14$) emerges from tensor product eigenvalue degeneracies of multi-electron atoms.

**Beta decay universality.**

Beta transitions between table entries are governed by a single universal matrix $\Delta_\beta(q)$ ([beta decay matrix](#prop:beta-decay-transfer-matrix)): the same $2 \times 2$ perturbation for every nucleus, regardless of partner nucleon type. The $\mathcal{Q}_q$-value of any decay is the difference of parent and daughter Skein polynomials, concentrated at the converting nucleon’s generators.

**Why $N > Z$ for heavy elements.** The neutron count $N$ exceeds $Z$ for all elements beyond calcium. In the QOU framework, proton–proton Hopf crossings carry a repulsive Skein phase (electromagnetic charge), while proton–neutron and neutron–neutron crossings are purely attractive (strong force only). The repulsive crossing penalty grows as $\sim Z^2$, requiring additional neutrons to stabilize the multi-nucleon link. Elements marked $\diamond$ have a proton stability pair; those marked $\star$ have a neutron stability pair. At these values the Skein polynomial has closed-shell structure with anomalously high $B/A$.

**Stability pairs**: $2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82$ (protons); $2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126$ (neutrons).

**Input parameters** (one free parameter): $q = q_0$, $\hbar_q \approx 0.09907$, $m_{\mathfrak{p}} \approx 938.269$ MeV, $m_{\mathfrak{n}} \approx 939.565$ MeV, $m_e \approx 0.511$ MeV.
